docs.text: Byrgenwerth Bloodborne Paleblood is a decompilation of Bloodborne with its own runtime, one verified function at a time We are born of the blood, made men by the blood, undone by the blood. Our eyes are yet to open… Fear the old blood. Master Willem / The Blood Minister Read the devlog Join the hunt Paleblood rewrites Bloodborne ( PS4 , CUSA03173, version 1.09) function by function as readable C++ that does exactly what the original did, and builds a runtime of its own for that code to run on. Where the hunt stands The game doesn't run on Paleblood yet: 21 of 157,757 functions are verified (0.01%). On our own runtime the executable's boot gets as far as scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (libkernel, called by libc.elf), with 252 of 686 system imports provided. 37% of imports System imports provided 252 of 686 imports the boot needs are provided. 219 come from the game's own modules and 33 from the runtime. Boot milestone: loaded (0 of 8). Start here The hunt Devlog What changed each week, mistakes included. Read Numbers Progress Replaced and verified functions, by system and address. See progress How it works Runtime Our own runtime and how far the game boots on it. Explore For hunters Contributing Your first pull request, and the rules that keep it clean. Get started A place to learn No console, dump or game files are needed to learn here: every page explains how the game's code works in our own words and our own code. How a console game fits together The executable, its libraries, the frame loop and the two tracks. Architecture The first system, step by step How the frame limiter paces the game, and how it was replaced. Frame limiter Reverse engineering in practice Reading disassembly, and the traps in the tools. Ghidra & PS4 quirks Every term, explained Hover a dotted term anywhere for its meaning. Glossary More about the project Why we do this, and the goal Because we love this game. Yharnam deserves to outlive the hardware it was made for, and to be understood as well as it is loved: every function of the original, read, named, rewritten and proved to behave exactly as it did, so that one day it runs natively, at any frame rate, for as long as there are hunters to play it. The goal is a complete source port of Bloodborne for the PC. When the hunt is over, every function of the game's 1.09 executable will have been rewritten as readable C++ and proved to behave exactly like the original, and the game will run natively on Paleblood's own runtime : no PS4 , no emulator, no original executable, only the game's data from your own copy. Because it will be source, the game can be read, understood, preserved, fixed and modded like any other program, at any frame rate and resolution. Two tracks get there, side by side: Decompilation: functions rewritten as readable C++ and proved against the original in the verification harness , on inputs recorded earlier and on generated edge cases . Runtime: our own loader (done), generic input capture (foundation in place; integration incomplete), kernel, threads and memory, files, input, audio, video out, and the graphics, rebuilt at the engine's own level rather than by emulating the PS4 's GPU ( Runtime ). The game does not run on Paleblood until the runtime is far enough along that road. Today the harness maps the executable and bundled modules, then stops during bundled libc startup at an unresolved system import, before the first boot milestone; full game runs still use an external host scaffold while the project-owned runtime is completed. How a function becomes verified Analyze. Ghidra with the GhidraOrbis loader finds the function in your own dump; its callers, callees and the memory it touches are read from the disassembly, not only the decompiler. Name. It gets a name and a system in the shared function table, so every contributor's Ghidra shows the same names. Rewrite. A readable C++ version: named structures instead of raw offsets, named calls instead of addresses, named constants, faithful to what the original does. Verify. The harness runs the original and the replacement on equivalent recorded and generated inputs, comparing ABI-selected results, preserved registers, declared memory state, and scripted library calls. Optional instruction tracing adds bounded access and control-flow observations; its limits are described in Architecture . Deliberately wrong versions must fail. Review. An independent reviewer checks the verification and the readability. A function whose code no recording reaches yet is edge-verified until one does. Key documents Document What it covers Architecture The two tracks, the verification harness , the frame pipeline Runtime Our own runtime : the roadmap and how far the game's executable boots on it How the Frame Limiter Works The first system replaced , step by step Glossary PS4 and project terms explained Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Traps in the tools and the ABI Contributing Joining, the first pull request, the rules The executable's code, slice by slice, is on the Address Map ; every tracked function with its status is on its system page . The devlog tells the story as it happened, mistakes included. Legal, and the target this project is built for This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony Interactive Entertainment or FromSoftware in any way. Tools and source only: no game files, no extracted assets, no decompiler dumps. Everything starts from your own console and your own copy: to contribute or verify you need Bloodborne (CUSA03173, EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from your own PS4 . The project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools. How to read it Density is relative to the densest slice. Hover a cell for its address range, function count and bytes. Only code is mapped. The code is one block from 0x00400000 ; read-only data, the exception tables and the writable data follow it and are not on the map. Addresses are not systems. The game's systems are spread across the executable; the system pages say which functions belong where. Small replacements stay visible. A slice with replaced code always gets a bar at least a little wide. Layout of the executable Range What 0x00400000 … Code ( .text ): every function the map shows after the code Read-only data, .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr (unwind tables) after that Writable data and zero-initialized data The exact block boundaries are the GhidraOrbis loader 's; see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks for how they were checked against the unwind tables.

docs.title: Address Map

docs.text: Density is relative to the densest slice. Hover a cell for its address range, function count and bytes. Only code is mapped. The code is one block from 0x00400000 ; read-only data, the exception tables and the writable data follow it and are not on the map. Addresses are not systems. The game's systems are spread across the executable; the system pages say which functions belong where. Small replacements stay visible. A slice with replaced code always gets a bar at least a little wide.

The decompilation rewrites the game's code, function by function, as readable C++ that is proved to behave like the original. The runtime is what that code, and the original executable while it is being replaced , runs on: Paleblood's own loader and a growing set of PS4 system-call implementations. The game does not run on Paleblood's runtime yet; the Runtime page has the roadmap, implemented calls, and the latest saved boot result. What runs where today Full game runs still use an external host scaffold while the project-owned runtime is completed. The verification harness independently maps the executable and replays recorded inputs. Its capture writer now supports stable, function/run-identified output and replay checks, but it has no production call sites yet and does not automatically provide new game inputs. Paleblood also has a project-owned implementation of the version-1 hook callback. A synthetic executable-memory test verifies that its jump reaches a replacement, but the callback is not yet wired into the full game-run scaffold and does not establish full-run equivalence. The decompilation track A replacement lives in the code repository's game/<system>/ and follows its style rules: the objects a function touches are structures with named fields; the original's other functions and globals are reached through named declarations, not addresses; constants are named; there is no test plumbing inside the game's code. A function reaches the main branch only when it is both verified and readable, and an independent reviewer, not the author, has checked both. How a replacement takes over. Replacements are registered in a hook table. When the runtime runs the game, each registered function's entry will jump to its replacement, so every caller lands in the new code. It is a 14-byte jump, which is why a function shorter than that cannot be hooked this way. The runtime track Load. Paleblood's loader maps the game's executable, together with the game's own C library and file system modules. Link. It applies every relocation and binds every system import, to one of those modules or to the runtime 's own implementation. Boot. The boot harness starts the guest startup sequence and stops at the first system function the runtime does not implement yet, naming it. Implement. The next piece of runtime work implements what the boot stopped at, written clean-room from public documentation and our own reverse engineering. The latest saved trace stops in the game's bundled libc before the executable reaches its first boot milestone. The frame pipeline The first system decompiled. Solid boxes are verified C++; dashed boxes are still original code. next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work Once per frame, the frame step: checks that the window is running; creates the SprjFlipper on the first frame (its constructor reads Game.FlipMode ); lets the flipper's limiter wait out the frame; runs the game's task update. The full walk-through is in How the Frame Limiter Works . Verification Earlier game runs inputs recorded while the game ran Edge-case generators what a recording does not reach Capture library captures/ / _NNNN.json harness.py our loader; original and replacement, same inputs verify.py compare returns, registers, bytes, calls Mutation test wrong variants must fail edge-verified, verified plus the independent review A replacement is checked against the original outside the game. Map. The harness maps the executable from your own dump with Paleblood's loader , and scripts every library call the function makes. Feed. The inputs are cases recorded in earlier game runs (the capture library) and edge cases generated for the corners. Run both. The original and the replacement run on the same inputs. Compare. ABI-selected return values, callee-saved registers, final bytes in declared memory regions, and scripted library calls must match. Break it on purpose. Deliberately wrong versions of the replacement must fail; if one passes, the cases are too weak and get fixed first. Status Meaning edge-verified Passes, but no recording reaches the function's code yet. verified Recordings for it exist and pass, and the independent review has approved it. What the automated tools can establish The merged differential engine adds deterministic fixture replay, bounded input exploration, mismatch minimization, and portable evidence reports. Its tests prove infrastructure behavior using synthetic instructions; they do not establish a new game function's semantics or promote a function automatically. Instruction tracing (optional, Linux) watches supported guest memory reads and writes at byte granularity, including unaligned accesses, aliased pointers, and writes that leave the same value. For each access it records: the instruction; the access range; the bytes before and after; the register context. Reading a difference. The first differing recorded memory event is a bounded diagnostic. Original and replacement code may take different instruction paths, so an internal trace difference with equal observable results is not treated as a behavior mismatch. Limits of instruction tracing The support matrix defines its limits: classified string/repeat, vector-memory, atomic, and system instructions fail closed; host code outside the instrumented ranges leaves an explicit gap. Capstone does not identify every architectural implicit-memory operation, so completeness applies only to the audited instruction families. The tool does not claim an exact first divergence of every register at every instruction. Coverage and the candidate pipeline Supported instruction traces record executed basic blocks and outgoing edges per fixture. Complete traces can prioritize seeds that found new edges, or a conditional outcome whose other outcome is still unseen. Partial and unavailable coverage remain explicit and cannot feed that ranking. This describes observed fixture paths, not a complete static map of every possible path. The opt-in automation prototype connects catalog qualification to an isolated worktree, local recorded fixtures, both compiler builds, differential tests, repository checks, and a reviewable draft pull request. It accepts a prewritten clean-room replacement patch; source generation is not automated. Each gate needs its evidence, and missing evidence rejects the run: Gate Evidence required Candidate Fresh ownership checks, replacement-development qualification, exact executable identity, and documented ABI. Fixtures Recorded-game provenance and sufficient matching cases; generated boundary cases supplement those recordings. Execution Matching observable results, complete supported instruction traces, valid memory accesses, and eligible CFG coverage. Delivery Compiler and repository checks, a reproducible evidence report, then GitHub CI and human review. What the pipeline has not shown Missing evidence rejects the run. Dry-run mode performs local work only, and a regression canary cannot open a function PR. No complete real-game candidate-to-PR run has been established by the merged evidence. Synthetic pipeline success does not change the verification counts . Addresses Every address in this wiki is a PS4 virtual address with the executable at 0x400000 , the convention of the community patches. See Ghidra & PS4 Quirks . What comes next The queues live in the code repository's NEXT.md : one for the decompilation track, one for the runtime track. Import-boundary observations PR #85 takes bounded snapshots of registers and selected stack/fixture-buffer bytes when the harness enters and returns from a recognized import. They show the net change at that boundary, and nothing more. What import-boundary snapshots do not show Merged PR #85 adds bounded snapshots of registers and selected stack/fixture-buffer bytes at recognized harness import entry and return. They expose net changes at that boundary; they do not trace host instructions, establish argument types, observe every memory access, or prove host control-flow coverage. Comparison, automation acceptance and coverage feedback continue to reject external-execution evidence even if another label incorrectly calls the trace complete. These diagnostics cannot qualify a function for verification, and the import-dependent clock regression remains incomplete.

docs.text: CI Setup Both repositories run GitHub Actions on every push and pull request. Neither ever sees game data: nothing from a dump is in the repositories, and CI does not need it. At a glance Code repository Build matrix (GCC, Clang), policy, and a session report on pull requests. Wiki Rejects game data, checks generated files, builds with --strict . Merge-blocking The four code repository checks, including the readable-code check. Runs locally only Function-level verification against the real game: it needs your dump. Code repository ( Paleblood ) .github/workflows/ci.yml runs three jobs: Job What it checks build (gcc) , build (clang) CMake build, the syslib CTest (RT_SYSLIB), the rest of CTest, and the Python suites. policy No game data, valid function tables, README progress, readable code, pre-commit hooks . session report On pull requests: picks the right report from the changed file paths. What each job does in full build (gcc) and build (clang) — install the pinned optional Capstone dependency, configure and build with CMake, run the syslib CTest (the RT_SYSLIB unit test), then run the remaining CTest suite. The workflow also runs the harness /instruction-trace and differential-engine Python suites with each compiler and its built loader . It includes hook -table and loader tests, the plug-in contract test, synthetic executable-memory hook tests, and synthetic tracing, CFG, and mutation regressions. These tests do not run the full game-run scaffold or establish native game-run equivalence. policy — rejects anything that looks like game data; validates the function tables; checks that runtime and tools name nothing specific to the game; checks that the README progress matches tools/progress.py ; runs the readable-code check (addresses, raw offsets, magic numbers, and recording code); and exercises the pre-commit hooks . session report — on pull requests, CI selects the concise report for runtime -only changes, the documentation report, or the full decompilation/mixed report from changed file paths. Unknown code paths fail closed to the full report. Runtime changes cannot downgrade a mixed PR. The build and policy jobs still apply to every path. These four checks are required by Paleblood's current main branch protection. Readability and independent review tools/check_readable.py (in policy ) is required and merge-blocking. A reviewer who did not write a function must approve it before it is verified . Function-level verification runs locally, not in CI. Readability check and review record The policy job's tools/check_readable.py step is a required, merge-blocking check. It rejects mechanical transcription patterns in game/ , and CI refuses any growth in the grandfathered-file list. The check does not judge whether names, structure, complexity, or comments are easy for people to follow. Before a function is marked verified , a reviewer who did not write it must assess both its verification evidence and readability; the approval is recorded in symbols/reviews.csv and the promotion tools validate that record. Paleblood's current branch protection does not require a blanket approving review on every pull request. Local verification, runtime PRs and promotion Function-level verification against the real game cannot run in CI, because it needs your dump. It remains required for decompilation changes and runs locally ( tools/verify.py run , tools/smoke.sh ). The full session report must include every replacement status change recorded for the PR and matching, non-empty, passing verify.py evidence for each replaced , edge-verified , or verified function. Runtime-only contributions do not require a dump, captures , or function-level verification. After a runtime PR merges, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts its result on the PR. tools/promote.py checks existing recorded and edge cases locally and requires an approved review before promotion. Comparison result files go to temporary storage; the capture library remains input-only. --dry-run leaves verification metadata and function status unchanged. Wiki ( Byrgenwerth ) .github/workflows/ci.yml installs MkDocs, rejects game data, checks that every generated file (progress data, tables, visuals) agrees with the data it comes from and that no page has a hand-typed count, builds the site with --strict , and exercises the pre-commit hooks . Local workflow (no CI needed) Shell tools/install_hooks.sh # both repositories tools/smoke.sh # code repository: the pipeline on a known function export BB_PORT_DIR = /absolute/path/to/clean-paleblood-main-at-merged-sha tools/end_session.sh # wiki: pull numbers from the code repository, build, check python3 -m mkdocs serve # wiki: preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 Pin BB_PORT_DIR for wiki validation For wiki validation and publication, pin BB_PORT_DIR to a clean worktree at the exact merged Paleblood revision and record its absolute path and full SHA in the shared checkpoint. Do not use the implicit sibling checkout when it may contain uncommitted or stale changes.

docs.text: Contributing Tonight, Gehrman joins the hunt. Gehrman, the First Hunter Paleblood is open to everyone. This is the short version: how to help, your first pull request, and the rules. Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Traps in the tools and the PS4 ABI that cost time. Read Glossary PS4 and project terms explained. Read CI Setup What runs on every push and pull request. Read Credits The tools and contributors the project stands on. Read Evidence & Media Review How claims are labelled and media is reviewed. Read Full rules: the code repository's CONTRIBUTING.md . Setup: its ONBOARDING.md . Questions: Discussions . Ways to help Track What you do Name functions Good first issues: name small, clear functions in the shared function table. Document a system One page here per system. Replace functions Readable C++ replacements, verified and reviewed. Build the runtime Implement PS4 system calls in RT_SYSLIB . No dump needed. Tooling The harness , the capture library, the Ghidra scripts. More on each track Name functions — the good first issues: small functions with a clear purpose, identified from their callers and the library calls they make, named in the shared function table. Document a system — a page here per system: summary, key functions, structures, patch points, open questions. Replace functions — readable C++ replacements, verified against the original with the harness and reviewed independently. Build the runtime — claim a call or tightly related group in its system issue ( #34–#41 ), then use a runtime/<function> branch to implement it in RT_SYSLIB with unit tests. Runtime-only work is clean-room, needs no game dump or captures , and receives maintainer boot verification after merge; see the runtime syscall notes and full workflow in Paleblood's contribution guide. Tooling — the harness , the capture library, the Ghidra scripts. Your first pull request Fork. Fork Paleblood and run tools/install_hooks.sh in your clone. Set up. Decompilation: follow ONBOARDING.md. Runtime: claim a function in its system issue (#34–#41) on a runtime/<function> branch. Keep it small. One function or tightly related group per PR, with RT_SYSLIB unit cases and a runtime report. Merge. CI runs without a dump. After merge, a maintainer boot-tests it and posts the result. Each step in full Fork Paleblood on GitHub and run tools/install_hooks.sh in your clone. For decompilation, follow ONBOARDING.md from your own dump to Ghidra . For runtime work, read the syscall notes and claim one function or related group in its system issue (#34–#41); use a branch named runtime/<function> . Keep one function or tightly related group per PR. Add RT_SYSLIB unit cases and include evidence, confirmed behavior, unresolved questions, and test results in the runtime report. Runtime-only PRs run the compiler matrix, RT_SYSLIB tests, and repository policy checks without requiring a dump, captures , or function-level verify.py . After merge, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts the result on the PR. Your own copy Decompilation needs your own PS4 and your own copy of the game. Runtime work needs no game files. The project never provides them. Your own copy in full Decompilation work starts from your own console and your own copy of the game: Bloodborne (CUSA03173, EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from your own PS4 . Runtime-only contributions do not need a dump, captures , or any game files. The project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools. Requests for game files, or links to them, are removed wherever they are posted, and may lead to a ban. Ground rules No game files. Ever. No game media in the code repository. Verified and readable before it is done. Say how you know. One pull request per function or cluster. The ground rules in full No game files. Ever. No executables, assets, decompiler output or extracted data in commits, issues, pull requests or Discussions. Keep game media out of Paleblood's code repository and its issues, pull requests, and Discussions. The documentation site follows a separate, asset-by-asset review process for technical and critical context; attribution or educational purpose alone does not establish permission. See Evidence & Media Review . Verified and readable. A replacement that "looks right" is not done until the harness finds no difference on recorded and edge cases , deliberately wrong versions fail, it reads well (the code repository's STYLE.md), and an independent reviewer has approved it. The local promotion tool reruns the recorded and edge suites before changing a function to verified ; its comparison output is temporary and kept away from the capture library. Case data stays on the contributor's machine. Say how you know. When you name a function, say how you inferred what it does: its callers, its library calls, the memory it touches. A name says what is known and no more. One pull request per function or cluster , with the disclosures CONTRIBUTING.md asks for.

Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Traps in the tools and the PS4 ABI that cost time. Read Glossary PS4 and project terms explained. Read CI Setup What runs on every push and pull request. Read Credits The tools and contributors the project stands on. Read Evidence & Media Review How claims are labelled and media is reviewed. Read Full rules: the code repository's CONTRIBUTING.md . Setup: its ONBOARDING.md . Questions: Discussions .
docs.title: Contributing

docs.text: Track What you do Name functions Good first issues: name small, clear functions in the shared function table. Document a system One page here per system. Replace functions Readable C++ replacements, verified and reviewed. Build the runtime Implement PS4 system calls in RT_SYSLIB . No dump needed. Tooling The harness , the capture library, the Ghidra scripts. More on each track Name functions — the good first issues: small functions with a clear purpose, identified from their callers and the library calls they make, named in the shared function table. Document a system — a page here per system: summary, key functions, structures, patch points, open questions. Replace functions — readable C++ replacements, verified against the original with the harness and reviewed independently. Build the runtime — claim a call or tightly related group in its system issue ( #34–#41 ), then use a runtime/<function> branch to implement it in RT_SYSLIB with unit tests. Runtime-only work is clean-room, needs no game dump or captures , and receives maintainer boot verification after merge; see the runtime syscall notes and full workflow in Paleblood's contribution guide. Tooling — the harness , the capture library, the Ghidra scripts.
docs.title: Ways to help

docs.text: Fork. Fork Paleblood and run tools/install_hooks.sh in your clone. Set up. Decompilation: follow ONBOARDING.md. Runtime: claim a function in its system issue (#34–#41) on a runtime/<function> branch. Keep it small. One function or tightly related group per PR, with RT_SYSLIB unit cases and a runtime report. Merge. CI runs without a dump. After merge, a maintainer boot-tests it and posts the result. Each step in full Fork Paleblood on GitHub and run tools/install_hooks.sh in your clone. For decompilation, follow ONBOARDING.md from your own dump to Ghidra . For runtime work, read the syscall notes and claim one function or related group in its system issue (#34–#41); use a branch named runtime/<function> . Keep one function or tightly related group per PR. Add RT_SYSLIB unit cases and include evidence, confirmed behavior, unresolved questions, and test results in the runtime report. Runtime-only PRs run the compiler matrix, RT_SYSLIB tests, and repository policy checks without requiring a dump, captures , or function-level verify.py . After merge, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts the result on the PR.
docs.title: Your first pull request

docs.text: Decompilation needs your own PS4 and your own copy of the game. Runtime work needs no game files. The project never provides them. Your own copy in full Decompilation work starts from your own console and your own copy of the game: Bloodborne (CUSA03173, EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from your own PS4 . Runtime-only contributions do not need a dump, captures , or any game files. The project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools. Requests for game files, or links to them, are removed wherever they are posted, and may lead to a ban.
docs.title: Your own copy

docs.text: No game files. Ever. No game media in the code repository. Verified and readable before it is done. Say how you know. One pull request per function or cluster. The ground rules in full No game files. Ever. No executables, assets, decompiler output or extracted data in commits, issues, pull requests or Discussions. Keep game media out of Paleblood's code repository and its issues, pull requests, and Discussions. The documentation site follows a separate, asset-by-asset review process for technical and critical context; attribution or educational purpose alone does not establish permission. See Evidence & Media Review . Verified and readable. A replacement that "looks right" is not done until the harness finds no difference on recorded and edge cases , deliberately wrong versions fail, it reads well (the code repository's STYLE.md), and an independent reviewer has approved it. The local promotion tool reruns the recorded and edge suites before changing a function to verified ; its comparison output is temporary and kept away from the capture library. Case data stays on the contributor's machine. Say how you know. When you name a function, say how you inferred what it does: its callers, its library calls, the memory it touches. A name says what is known and no more. One pull request per function or cluster , with the disclosures CONTRIBUTING.md asks for.

docs.text: Evidence & Media Review How pages label evidence, and how any image or clip gets reviewed before it appears on this site. At a glance Label it Name the evidence type behind each claim, and link the exact source. Not evidence Merging a pull request or closing an issue does not show that game execution advanced. Review each asset Every image or clip needs its own provenance and rights review before it is copied or published. Credit ≠ permission Attribution and educational intent are context; neither alone grants permission. Code repository No game media there at all. A review for this site does not change that. How to read a claim Byrgenwerth explains how Bloodborne works from evidence gathered by Paleblood and its contributors. A test result, a trace, and a gameplay observation answer different questions, so pages label them separately. Evidence label What it supports What it does not establish by itself Verified original-game behavior A Paleblood replacement matched the original on the recorded and edge cases listed in its verification record, with independent review. Every possible input or every game state. Direct static analysis A behavior or relationship visible in disassembly, callers, data references, or a readable replacement. That a code path ran in an observed play session. Recorded original-game observation What happened in an original-game run or captured call, for the recorded conditions. Unobserved states or the reason behind an outcome. Synthetic Paleblood test The tested Paleblood infrastructure or function behavior under the synthetic fixture. Original-game execution or a real production capture . Paleblood-owned infrastructure A project-created loader , host interface, diagnostic, test, or tool and its demonstrated behavior. That the full game uses or reaches it. External research A cited fact or interpretation from a named outside source. Independent confirmation by Paleblood. Hypothesis / open question A plausible interpretation that guides further investigation. A confirmed function purpose or game rule. When a claim combines evidence types, say which part each type supports. Combining and citing evidence When a claim combines evidence types, state which part each type supports. Link to the exact source revision, test record, or published source that supports it. Merging a pull request or closing an issue is not evidence that game execution advanced. Screenshots, clips, and other media Use as little as possible: the smallest portion and resolution that explains the point. Never publish extracted assets, proprietary captures , bulk game text, secrets, or unsourced material. No retired or borrowed images presented as Paleblood output. The media rule in full The public documentation site may use an individual image or short clip when it materially helps explain a technical point, or supports criticism, research, or commentary. Each proposed asset needs its own provenance and rights review before it is copied into this private source or published. Attribution and educational intent are relevant context; neither alone grants permission. The review must identify the source, creator and rights holder where known, intended use, amount shown, attribution terms, permission or license (or a reasoned, asset-specific legal basis for the proposed use), privacy and security concerns, accessibility text, resizing or redaction, and maintainer approval. Use only the smallest portion and resolution that explains the point. Do not publish extracted assets, proprietary captures , bulk game text, secrets, or material whose source cannot be established. Do not republish retired image collections or describe another project's screenshots as Paleblood output. The code repository has a stricter rule The Paleblood code repository has its own stricter rule: game screenshots, clips, extracted assets, game files, and decompiler output do not belong in its source, issues, pull requests, or Discussions. A media review for this site does not authorize placing media in the code repository. Current media record Asset Status Bloodborne menu artwork in the sidebar Displayed with maintainer approval; rights unresolved Original SVG diagram Paleblood-owned, no game imagery Retired gallery Absent Attribution and a link to the source entry are on the Credits page. The sidebar artwork: display, provenance and rights The site menu shows the 256×256 Bloodborne menu artwork credited to r_dsgnd on SteamGridDB. It appears once per page as a small image at the top of the sidebar, above the section's links (on the homepage, above the Home link), shown as a banner 120 pixels tall cropped from the square picture, with descriptive alt text. Its contributor/source attribution and a link to the source entry are on the Credits page. The private asset record explains the supplied file's provenance and pixel match to the former wiki icon, intended display size, copyright rationale, and unresolved rights status. No license for redistribution of the underlying game artwork was found; contributor credit and the educational/research context are not treated as permission or as a guarantee of an exception. The maintainer approved this specific display through the review-and-merge workflow; the unresolved rights assessment remains recorded privately. The retired gallery remains absent. An original SVG diagram elsewhere in the encyclopedia is Paleblood-owned and contains no game imagery. Where the detailed records are kept Maintainers keep the detailed per-asset record privately; those records are not included in the generated website.

docs.text: Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Grant us eyes, grant us eyes! Plant eyes on our brains, to cleanse our beastly idiocy! Micolash, Host of the Nightmare Traps in the tools and the PS4 ABI that cost time. This page is the code repository's QUIRKS.md , copied in by tools/sync_progress.py , so the two never disagree. Traps in Ghidra and the PS4 ABI that cost time. Entries marked unconfirmed come from general PS4 / Orbis knowledge and have not been checked on this target yet; confirm or correct them when you hit them. The converted executable The ELF has no section headers (confirmed). The Orbis loader ( GhidraOrbis ) synthesizes blocks from the program headers: the executable PT_LOAD becomes .text , and its own heuristic splits .rodata , .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr off the end of it. The progress denominator is the functions Ghidra finds in that .text block, so it depends on the loader and the analysis. progress.py ties its numbers to the hash of the committed export, and the export prints how many functions fell outside .text . .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr are marked executable by the loader ; they are data. e_type is 0xfe10 (confirmed), not ET_EXEC or ET_DYN . The first PT_LOAD has p_vaddr 0, so the file does not say where the game lives; the convention below does. Ghidra 's default for this file type is unconfirmed : always set the image base explicitly on import and check it (the export script refuses any other base). Program headers include Sony types ( PT_SCE_* , PT_SCE_DYNLIBDATA and friends) that Ghidra does not understand. The PT_INTERP is /libexec/ld-elf.so.1 (confirmed). Dynamic linking data is in a Sony-specific segment, so Ghidra will not resolve imports by itself. SelfUtil-Patched removes the repeated data before the first segment (at 0x4000) and patches the version segment. Another SelfUtil build can produce a different file with different hashes: always check target.sha256 , and check the loaded image too ( target.image.sha256 ), which no build choice changes. The v1.09 executable is not region-specific (confirmed 2026-10-11). Evidence: a US package - CUSA00900 , content id UP9000-CUSA00900_00-BLOODBORNE000000 , app version 1.09 merged over the base, region and title id read from sce_sys/param.sfo - converted with the pinned SelfUtil build ( tools/selfutil/build.sh , commit 53ca642b ) into ELFs that reproduce every hash in target.sha256 : eboot.elf ca8813862d7b1345… and all seven system modules. It also reproduces the build-independent loaded image in target.image.sha256 , 071df19c8880086d… . tools/check_target.py <elf-dir> prints the nine ok lines. So the hashes decide whether a dump lines up with our addresses; the title id does not. Two corollaries: a pre-patched executable (a frame-rate or debug-menu repack) breaks the loaded-image pin, so that pin doubles as an integrity check; and an untested region or version (JP CUSA00208 , any other AppVer) stays unknown until its own check says ok . Address conventions All addresses in this repository are PS4 virtual addresses: the ELF p_vaddr plus 0x400000 , with Ghidra 's image base set to 0x400000 . Community patch files use the same address convention. Three conventions exist, one constant apart. V is the ELF p_vaddr . Convention Address Where it appears ELF virtual address V ELF program headers and file layout PS4 virtual address V + 0x400000 ours , Ghidra , community patch files To convert an address to the ELF virtual address, subtract 0x400000 . tools/validate_functions.py rejects any address below 0x00400000 , which catches a base-0 import by mistake. Checked against the target image (read-only): - The community "Performance Patch" address 0x0261B108 minus 0x400000 holds c7 45 b4 06 00 00 00 ( mov dword [rbp-0x4c], 6 ), which the patch changes to 9. Tool-independent identity: the loaded image (loadable segments copied to their p_vaddr , SHA-256) of this target is 071df19c8880086d97182dbc057bc8cb37badaca57d9112683836b24a0444c0a . It is the same whichever SelfUtil build produced the ELF . Ghidra itself Ghidra 12 headless has no Jython: a .py script fails with " Ghidra was not started with PyGhidra". Our scripts are Java GhidraScripts. support/analyzeHeadless hardcodes MAXMEM=2G . That is too small for this binary; raise it in that file (setup in docs/GHIDRA.md). The Orbis loader replaces an image base of 0 by 0x1000000 by default. Pass -loader-imageBase 0x400000 ( -loader-baseAddr is ignored by this loader ). -loader "Orbis ELF" is rejected by headless as an invalid loader name; leave -loader out, the Orbis loader is picked automatically for this file. Ghidra 12.1.4's VEX VSQRTSS and VSQRTSD rules reverse the two source roles. The low result must be the square root of source 2 (ModRM), with the upper lanes from source 1 (VEX.vvvv), as specified in Intel's instruction manual . For vsqrtss xmm1,xmm0,xmm1 , distinct low inputs 9 and 25 must produce 5, retaining XMM0's upper lanes. The stock rules produce 3 and retain XMM1's upper lanes. This was checked with synthetic single/double probes in the x86-64 verification VM and through REA before and after correcting an isolated private SDK copy. The original SDK remains intact; record the modified SLEIGH/SLA hashes and start a fresh REA output directory when using the correction. The follow camera update and pitch getter contain affected instructions. Instruction coverage alone does not establish correct decompiler semantics. Calling convention Orbis uses the System V AMD64 ABI: integer arguments in rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9 , floats in xmm0-xmm7 , return in rax:rdx / xmm0:xmm1 , callee-saved rbx rbp r12-r15 . Variadic callers set al to the number of vector registers. Leaf functions use the 128-byte red zone below rsp . Ghidra 's stack analysis can read that as unused or mis-size the frame. Optimized code splits and merges functions (tail calls, shared epilogues, cold paths in the same range). A "function" boundary in Ghidra may be wrong. Check the call sites before you claim a size. Parameters Ghidra types as undefined8 are often pointers or floats in another register class. Read the call sites, not the decompiler's signature. Ghidra can pick a wrong calling convention for functions that pass a struct or this in an unusual register. Fix the signature before trusting the output. CPU The CPU is an AMD Jaguar: SSE up to 4.2, AVX and F16C, BMI1. No AVX2, BMI2 or FMA3 ( unconfirmed ). Ghidra 's decompiler does not model every instruction; an unaff_* or CONCAT expression is a sign to read the disassembly. Float comparisons that look odd ( ucomiss plus parity checks) encode NaN handling that the replacement has to keep. Imports and system calls Library calls are linked by NID (a hash of the symbol name), not by name. Ghidra shows stubs. Names come from public NID databases, not from the binary. Unconfirmed for this target's import layout. System calls go through the libkernel wrappers; rax holds the syscall number. Hooks The hook is a 14-byte absolute jump ( jmp [rip+0] plus the target) written over the start of the original function. Shorter functions cannot be hooked that way. Nothing may jump into the first 14 bytes of a hooked function from elsewhere: check the references to the function's start region in Ghidra before hooking. A replacement calls library functions through the game's own thunks (declared with RT_ORIGINAL ), not through host libraries, so whatever answers the original's calls (the verification harness 's stubs, or the runtime ) answers the replacement's the same way. Verification traps A replacement that returns the same value can still differ in memory writes. Write order does not matter but final bytes do: verify.py compares the final byte map. Uninitialized padding in structs is copied by the original. Replacement code that zeroes padding fails verify.py on memory writes; decide per case and record it in the function's note. Ghidra hides code after the engine's fatal error call Ghidra marks the engine's fatal error function ( 0x024b55b0 , "file, line, message") as non-returning, so the bytes after a call to it are not disassembled unless something jumps there. The game's code does continue there (a jump to the return, or to another report), which matters when a replacement is tested with that function stubbed. If a draft's disassembly has a gap after such a call, disassemble the bytes directly (objdump on the ELF ) before writing the replacement. Example: kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ) returns -3 after the EINVAL report. Replay overlapping community patch writes in order The community XML at commit e344639 contains overlapping Uncap FPS++ writes inside 0x02713870 . A five-byte call write at 0x02715d71 is partly overwritten by a later write starting at 0x02715d75 . The resulting instruction calls 0xffffffff917166f7 ; analyzing the first write alone gives the wrong target. A still later edit at 0x02713d76 replaces the incoming stock branch with a live path that loads SprjFlipper::frame_seconds , applies scalar min with 1/30 s, and jumps past the malformed residual code to 0x02715d79 . Direct intraprocedural control-flow walking finds no reachable incoming edge to the malformed call. This does not establish the absence of unknown external jumps. The invalid-owner route instead reads 0x0575a908 , initialized by this patch to bits 0x3c088889 (1/120 s). A replacement must reproduce the reachable patched routes, including their float operand order, rather than keep the stock time step because one isolated edit looks invalid. Retain the exact XML revision and replay all its writes before reasoning about option coverage; other revisions may differ.

docs.text: A replacement that returns the same value can still differ in memory writes. Write order does not matter but final bytes do: verify.py compares the final byte map. Uninitialized padding in structs is copied by the original. Replacement code that zeroes padding fails verify.py on memory writes; decide per case and record it in the function's note.
docs.title: Verification traps

docs.text: Ghidra marks the engine's fatal error function ( 0x024b55b0 , "file, line, message") as non-returning, so the bytes after a call to it are not disassembled unless something jumps there. The game's code does continue there (a jump to the return, or to another report), which matters when a replacement is tested with that function stubbed. If a draft's disassembly has a gap after such a call, disassemble the bytes directly (objdump on the ELF ) before writing the replacement. Example: kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ) returns -3 after the EINVAL report.
docs.title: Ghidra hides code after the engine's fatal error call

docs.text: The community XML at commit e344639 contains overlapping Uncap FPS++ writes inside 0x02713870 . A five-byte call write at 0x02715d71 is partly overwritten by a later write starting at 0x02715d75 . The resulting instruction calls 0xffffffff917166f7 ; analyzing the first write alone gives the wrong target. A still later edit at 0x02713d76 replaces the incoming stock branch with a live path that loads SprjFlipper::frame_seconds , applies scalar min with 1/30 s, and jumps past the malformed residual code to 0x02715d79 . Direct intraprocedural control-flow walking finds no reachable incoming edge to the malformed call. This does not establish the absence of unknown external jumps. The invalid-owner route instead reads 0x0575a908 , initialized by this patch to bits 0x3c088889 (1/120 s). A replacement must reproduce the reachable patched routes, including their float operand order, rather than keep the stock time step because one isolated edit looks invalid. Retain the exact XML revision and replay all its writes before reasoning about option coverage; other revisions may differ.

docs.text: Glossary: PS4 and port terms A running glossary for terms used across the devlog and the system pages. Hover any of them on another page for a short definition. The project Functional decompilation Rewriting the game's code as readable source that behaves exactly like the original, checked by running both on the same inputs. A matching decompilation goes further and requires the rebuilt bytes to be identical; this project does not, because the goal is a native port, not the original binary. What it does require is that every replaced function does the same thing: the same return value, the same memory written, the same calls made. Source port The game rebuilt from source to run natively somewhere else, here on a PC. It is where Paleblood is headed, not what it is today: the game does not run on Paleblood until its own runtime is far enough along. Hook A 14-byte jump written over the first bytes of an original function, pointing at the replacement. Every caller still calls the original address and lands in the replacement. A function shorter than the jump cannot be hooked this way. The hook table is installed by the runtime once it runs the game; the verification harness calls replacements directly. Thunk A tiny piece of code that only forwards a call. The game calls each PS4 library function through a thunk ; our replacements call the same thunks , so whatever answers the original's calls (the harness 's scripted stubs, or the runtime ) answers the replacement's the same way. Verification Replaced, edge-verified and verified A function is replaced once it is registered for hooking and the game library builds. It is edge-verified once its generated edge cases match the original instructions. It is verified once matching recorded-game cases also pass, mutation tests reject known wrong versions, and an independent reviewer approves the evidence and readability. These labels describe the recorded evidence, not every possible input or game state. tools/promote.py reruns the required cases and checks the review record before promotion; it does not create captures or supply approval. Harness, captures and edge cases The harness runs the original function from your own dump and its replacement, natively, outside the game, on the same inputs. Captures are inputs recorded while the game ran (the existing library was recorded on the old borrowed runtime ; Paleblood's own recorder now has a stable, self-identifying output format, but still needs production call sites); edge cases are generated for situations a short run does not reach. Mutation test Deliberately wrong versions of a replacement go through verification too: each must fail. If one passes, the cases cannot see that difference, and they are fixed before anything is called verified . Instruction trace and CFG coverage An instruction trace records supported memory accesses made while single-stepping a bounded fixture. A control-flow graph (CFG) describes blocks and the edges between them; dynamic CFG coverage records only the blocks and edges that the fixture actually reached. Complete supported coverage, partial coverage, and unavailable coverage are different outcomes. A skipped host call or unsupported instruction cannot be treated as a complete trace. See Architecture: Verification for the guarantees and limits. Runtime Runtime and loader The runtime is what the game's code runs on: Paleblood's own loader , which maps the executable and the game's own C library and file system modules and binds every system import, and its own versions of the PS4 system libraries, written clean-room. The project-owned runtime does not yet run the full game; see Runtime . Boot milestone and import coverage The runtime track measures how far the game's executable gets on Paleblood's own runtime . Import coverage distinguishes imports supplied by bundled guest modules, imports implemented by Paleblood, registered unresolved diagnostics, and unbound imports. The dashboard reports the last saved boot; registry changes alone do not refresh it. A boot milestone records a reached stage in startup, such as entry, threads, files, input, audio, video out, GPU, or first flip. The boot harness names the first unresolved call or execution failure. PS4 platform PS4, Orbis The PlayStation 4 runs an AMD x86-64 CPU (Jaguar) and Orbis OS, derived from FreeBSD. Because the CPU is x86-64 like a PC's, the game's code can run directly on a PC once something provides the operating system around it. SELF, ELF, PRX, eboot An ELF is the standard executable format of Linux and FreeBSD. The PS4 wraps executables in a SELF (signed ELF ); ours are fake-signed and unencrypted, so turning them back into ELFs only unwraps them. The main executable is eboot.bin ; PRX files are the PS4 's shared libraries. NID PS4 programs link to library functions by NID : a hash of the function's name. GhidraOrbis carries a database that turns NIDs back into names, so sceKernelUsleep shows up instead of a hash. FDE A Frame Description Entry: one function's unwind record in the executable's .eh_frame . Counting them gave an independent check on how many functions Ghidra found. GNM, PM4, GCN GNM is the PS4 's low-level graphics API; the game builds PM4 command packets for its AMD GCN graphics chip. Paleblood does not plan to emulate that chip: the graphics are to be rebuilt at the level of the game's own graphics layer, on Vulkan. vblank and flip The screen refreshes at a fixed rate; the gap between two refreshes is the vertical blank. A flip shows a finished frame at a vblank . The frame limiter can flip every vblank (60 frames a second on a 60 Hz screen) or every other one (30).

docs.text: How the Frame Limiter Works The first system of Bloodborne replaced in C++ is the one that decides how long each frame lasts. This page walks through it as the original does it, and as the replacement now does it, exactly the same way. At a glance When At the start of every frame, before the game's frame of work. Job Make sure the previous frame took long enough. Input One configuration value, Game.FlipMode . How it waits By spinning on the clock: precise, and it keeps one CPU core busy. next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work Where it sits Every frame, frame_timing_frame_step runs this sequence: Check. It asks the window whether the game is still running. Create, once. On the very first frame it creates the game's frame-pacing object, the SprjFlipper . Its constructor, frame_timing_flipper_init , reads one value from the game's configuration: Game.FlipMode . Pace. It calls the flipper's limiter, frame_timing_pace_frame . Work. Only after the limiter returns does the game do its frame of work. So the limiter runs at the start of every frame, and its job is to make sure the previous frame took long enough. Choosing the pace The flip mode picks one of five settings. Each sets two things in the flipper: the frame interval : a float, in seconds; the sync interval : how many vblanks a flip waits for. Mode Frame interval Sync interval 0, 1 1/30 s 2 2 1/60 s 1 3, 4 1/30 s 1 A pending mode can replace the current one at the start of a frame; a few flags reset the pacing state, for example after a load. Waiting out the frame The limiter reads the time with gettimeofday , works out how much of the frame's budget is left, and waits. The game carries two ways of waiting: Wait How it works Sleep, then spin Sleeps in chunks and spins the last few milliseconds. Spin only Reads the clock again and again until the time is up. A switch compiled into this build always picks the spinning one. That is why a quick frame can read the clock hundreds of thousands of times. It is precise, and it keeps one CPU core busy. The budget adapts. It is not always the full interval. The flipper keeps the last 32 frame times in a ring, marking the frames that ran late. If recent frames ran over, the next budget is shortened to catch up, but never below a third of the interval. Afterwards Once the wait is over, the limiter: records the frame's time in the ring; decides whether this frame counts as late, and if so drops the sync interval to 0 so the next flip does not wait for a vblank ; keeps a 16-frame history, from which it computes the frame rate the game reports; if a flag asks for it, tells another object that the game now targets 60 frames a second. The replacement The C++ version follows the original instruction by instruction, including how it converts between integers and floating point and how each comparison treats a value that is not a number. It also carries the port's first setting, BB_TARGET_FPS : BB_TARGET_FPS Effect unset Nothing changes. 30 A fixed interval of 1/30 s, no overrides. 60 A fixed interval of 1/60 s, no overrides. uncapped A fixed interval of 1/240 s, no overrides. The set values do what the community frame-rate patches do here, and the frame step passes the game the real frame time, as those patches do. See the frame timing page . How the replacement was checked It was compared with the original on every frame recorded in two game runs, including frames that spin on the clock for hundreds of thousands of reads, and on hand-written cases for every mode and flag; four deliberately wrong versions all failed. Each part of BB_TARGET_FPS is checked against the patch itself.

docs.text: Runtime call reference The runtime's own detailed notes on each system call: the evidence, the exact behavior and what stops by name. This page is copied from Paleblood's docs/runtime-syscalls.md every time the wiki syncs, so it always matches the code. For the reader-friendly explanation of the same calls, start with Runtime system calls . This page records contracts used to implement small runtime calls in issues #34 and #41 . Public standards and manuals describe portable or platform-specific API behavior; they do not by themselves prove every detail of the PS4 implementation. Keep the distinction below, and leave unresolved behavior unresolved until public documentation, our own reverse engineering, or observed behavior settles it. Evidence in this repository The runtime registry distinguishes behavior it implements from diagnostics for behavior that is still unknown. RT_SYSLIB entries are callable implementations and count toward coverage; RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED entries remain callable so a reached import can fail with a useful name, but do not count as implemented or as supplied imports in progress reports. symbols/imports.csv records getpagesize and gettimeofday as imports of eboot from libScePosix ; libc.elf imports clock_gettime , getpagesize , getpid , and gettimeofday from libkernel . Import rows establish that the names are required, not their arguments, return values at every call site, or all clock IDs. The eight hash- verified target images ( eboot.elf and the seven modules, tools/check_target.py ) all state p_align 0x4000 for every PT_LOAD segment, with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000 (the difference is exactly 0x4000 in each; readelf -l prints the headers). The decompiled frame limiter calls gettimeofday with a null timezone argument. A separate verified clock helper calls sceKernelClockGettime with clock ID 4 , named CLOCK_MONOTONIC in that code. This confirms one monotonic clock request in the game; it does not establish every ID passed through the imported clock_gettime wrapper, or that no other ID is used in unexamined code. Interfaces and known behavior Function Arguments and representation Publicly documented result and errors Evidence and open questions for PS4 getpagesize(void) No arguments. Returns the target's page size in bytes. The numeric value is platform-specific. getpagesize is not in current POSIX; portable code is directed to sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) . Linux and FreeBSD document the byte count; their manuals do not define a general error return for this function. Linux exposes it as a libc interface, not necessarily a dedicated kernel syscall. FreeBSD notes the system page size may differ from the underlying hardware page size. The import is present twice ( eboot from libScePosix , libc.elf from libkernel ), so both library names are registered against one implementation. The target images bound the value but do not pick one: every PT_LOAD of the eight hash- verified ELFs has p_align 0x4000 with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000, and the ELF ABI's congruence rule then limits the system page size to a divisor of 16384 (4096, 8192 or 16384); p_align is the alignment the image requires, not the page size the system reports. Stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096, and Sony's open-source page confirms the FreeBSD kernel is used but publishes the upstream sources, not the console's modifications, so no public source names the PS4 's own value. The runtime entry is therefore registered with RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED , so a boot that reaches it names the call, and it does not count as implemented ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). What would settle it: one observed getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) result on a console, or a guest call site whose page arithmetic shows the granularity the system uses. See the section "getpagesize: observed, inferred, unknown" below; do not hard-code the build host's page size. getpid(void) No arguments. Returns a pid_t naming the calling process. POSIX specifies that it succeeds and has no error return. Linux process IDs are scoped by PID namespaces; other systems have their own process-ID scope and lifecycle rules. The import is present, but this repository does not establish the guest-visible process ID or its scope. Returning the host PID is not justified by the API contract alone. clock_gettime(clock_id, tp) clock_id selects a clock; tp points to a struct timespec . On the POSIX interface, tv_sec is seconds and tv_nsec is nanoseconds in [0, 1,000,000,000) . The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. POSIX uses 0 for success and -1 with errno for failure. An unsupported clock ID is an EINVAL case. Linux and BSD manuals document additional pointer-error details; use the target contract rather than assuming the host's errno mapping. The imported wrapper is present. The verified sceKernelClockGettime call requests ID 4 ( CLOCK_MONOTONIC ). That is evidence for the SCE entry point only, not proof of the libc wrapper's IDs. Other IDs and exact PS4 error and pointer handling remain unresolved. Unknown IDs must not silently return a fabricated time. gettimeofday(tv, tz) tv points to a struct timeval : seconds since the Epoch and microseconds in [0, 1,000,000) . The historical timezone argument is passed as null at the confirmed game call site. The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. The wall clock can jump and is not a monotonic elapsed-time source. Historical POSIX specified a zero return on success and left errors undefined; Linux documents -1 / EFAULT for inaccessible pointers and ignores the timezone argument. POSIX.1-2024 removed the interface. The imported wrapper and game call sites are present; the game passes null for the second argument. Exact target behavior for bad pointers, non-null timezone arguments, and error mapping is not established. Do not silently ignore an error without evidence. sched_yield(void) No arguments. Returns int . POSIX: the calling thread gives up the processor until it is again at the head of its thread list; 0 on success, -1 with errno otherwise, and POSIX defines no error case for it. FreeBSD documents the same call. Imported by libc.elf from libkernel . Implemented: a guest thread runs on a host thread, so the runtime yields the host thread and returns 0 ( runtime/syslib/kernel_thread.c ). A host failure has no FreeBSD error number to report, so it stops by name. Not observable in a unit test: that the host scheduler actually ran another thread. scePthreadYield Asks for the same yield through the thread library. The PS4 -visible signature is not established. FreeBSD's pthread_yield(3) is void ; Linux's is int (always 0 ). No PS4 -specific public source gives the SCE name's declaration. Imported by eboot and libc.elf from libkernel ; no call site in this repository shows whether the caller reads a result. Registered with RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED : the entry stops by name and does not count as implemented. What would settle it: a guest call site showing whether the return register is read after the call, or a PS4 -specific public declaration. Do not assume an int or 0 from the FreeBSD or Linux analogues. memcpy(dest, src, n) , memset(dest, c, n) (libSceLibcInternal) void *memcpy(void *, const void *, size_t) and void *memset(void *, int, size_t) , the ISO C declarations. ISO C 7.24.2.1 and 7.24.6.1: memcpy copies n bytes from src to dest ; memset writes c converted to unsigned char into the first n bytes; both return dest . Overlapping memcpy regions and null pointers are undefined behaviour. Imported by libSceFios2.elf from libSceLibcInternal ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented with the host's own functions, since the standard fixes the whole result and no target-specific value is involved ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not modelled: what the PS4 C library does for the undefined cases; no public source or call site establishes it. sceKernelUsleep(microseconds) (libkernel), usleep(microseconds) (libScePosix) One unsigned 32-bit count of microseconds, returning int . For sceKernelUsleep the guest fixes the shape: the verified call sites in game/frame_timing/frame_limiter.cpp and game/render/swap_chain_present.cpp declare it as int(uint32_t microseconds) , and their cases expect 0 . FreeBSD's useconds_t is 32-bit unsigned. FreeBSD usleep(3) : suspends the thread for the given microseconds, 0 on success, -1 with EINTR if a signal interrupts it. SUSv2 also let usleep fail with EINVAL from 1,000,000 on; FreeBSD and POSIX.1-2008 (which removed usleep ) have no such limit. sceKernelUsleep is imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf , usleep by eboot . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested time and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Open: usleep with 1,000,000 or more, which stops by name because no PS4 -specific source says whether the guest sleeps or gets EINVAL ; and the SCE error, if any, for sceKernelUsleep , which the guest's sites never check. scePthreadRwlockInit(rwlock, attr, name) , scePthreadRwlockDestroy(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockRdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockWrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTryrdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTrywrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockUnlock(rwlock) (libkernel) A pointer to the guest's rwlock variable ( Init also an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); each returns int32_t . No call site in this repository shows these shapes; they come from the public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declarations, supporting evidence for the shapes only, and match FreeBSD's pthread_rwlock_* . POSIX pthread_rwlock_* , as FreeBSD libthr ( thr_rwlock.c ) and the kernel's umtx read-write lock ( kern_umtx.c ) implement it: a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use and a destroyed rwlock holding 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed rwlock; EBUSY from the try forms when the lock is not available; destroying does not check whether the lock is held, and leaves an unused initializer in place; unlocking is EPERM when another thread holds the write lock or when nobody holds the lock, and readers are counted, not named; a thread that locks again while holding the write lock is not given an error, it waits forever (no owner check in do_rw_wrlock or do_rw_rdlock ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. Imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf ( Tryrdlock by libSceFios2.elf only; symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented on a host rwlock that also records the writer and the reader count, which the host does not expose, for the unlock answers ( runtime/syslib/kernel_rwlock.c ). A missing variable answers EINVAL , as the mutex calls do; unlocking a never-used initializer is EPERM , as for the mutex. Stops by name: Rdlock or Wrlock while the caller holds the write lock (the system would wait forever, the host answers EDEADLK ; neither is useful to return), and an attribute object passed to Init (no imported call creates one, so its contents are not established; an empty attribute variable means the defaults, as in libthr). Not part of this entry: scePthreadRwlockTimedrdlock and Timedwrlock (imported by eboot ; only OpenOrbis gives their microsecond timeout, no call site does) and the libScePosix names. __stack_chk_fail(void) (libkernel) No arguments, no result: void __stack_chk_fail(void) , and it never returns (LSB; FreeBSD libc declares it __dead2 ). Compiler-generated code calls it, not application code. LSB Core: the function that called it is aborted with a message that a stack overflow was detected, and the program then exits. FreeBSD libc logs "stack overflow detected; terminated" and ends the process with SIGABRT . Imported by eboot , libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented as a stop by name ( rt_fatal , which aborts): ending the program is the whole guest-visible contract, so the entry counts as implemented ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not covered: the PS4 's own message or crash report, which the guest cannot observe after it ends; and __stack_chk_guard , a separate data import whose PS4 value is not established (an unbound data import gets a zeroed page, runtime/boot.c ). scePthreadCondInit(cond, attr, name) , scePthreadCondDestroy(cond) , scePthreadCondSignal(cond) , scePthreadCondBroadcast(cond) , scePthreadCondWait(cond, mutex) , scePthreadCondTimedwait(cond, mutex, microseconds) (libkernel) Pointers to the guest's cond and mutex variables; each returns int32_t . The guest fixes the wait shapes: the verified game/kernel/condition_wait.cpp declares Wait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex) and Timedwait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex, uint32_t timeout_us) , a relative timeout in microseconds, not POSIX's absolute timespec . The public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declares all six with these shapes ( Init with an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); it is supporting evidence for the shapes only. POSIX pthread_cond_* , as FreeBSD libthr implements it ( thr_cond.c ): a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use; a destroyed cond holds 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed cond; EBUSY to destroy one with waiters; destroying an unused initializer succeeds and leaves it in place; EPERM when the waiter does not own the mutex, for every mutex type, EINVAL when the mutex is destroyed ( _mutex_owned , thr_mutex.c ); ETIMEDOUT when a timed wait expires; a recursive mutex is released completely for the wait and its count restored after ( _mutex_cv_unlock , _mutex_cv_lock ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. scePthreadCondWait and Timedwait are imported by eboot , libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf , the other four by libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf ( symbols/imports.csv ). The guest's call site checks exactly 0x80020001 (EPERM), 0x80020016 (EINVAL) and 0x8002003c (ETIMEDOUT). Clock IDs and platform differences The only clock ID confirmed by a decompiled game call in this repository is 4 , used with sceKernelClockGettime and identified there as CLOCK_MONOTONIC . This does not prove that the game passes 4 to the imported clock_gettime wrapper. POSIX defines clock identifiers symbolically; their numeric values are implementation-specific. Linux adds clocks such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME ; FreeBSD has its own clock set, including CLOCK_UPTIME variants. Their names and numeric values are not interchangeable evidence for PS4 behavior. CLOCK_MONOTONIC represents elapsed time from an unspecified starting point and is not the wall clock. The precise effects of suspend, rate correction, and resolution vary by implementation. gettimeofday and CLOCK_REALTIME represent wall time tied to the Epoch and can move when system time changes. No source examined here establishes that the game asks the imported clock_gettime wrapper for CLOCK_REALTIME , CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW , CLOCK_BOOTTIME , or another ID. Public PSP2SDK API declarations provide those widths for the SCE names. The standard byte-order contract converts host order to network (big-endian) order for hton* , and reverses that conversion for ntoh* ; this is documented by the FreeBSD byte-order manual . Paleblood's guest ABI is AMD64, so these four conversions are byte reversals. Their implementations do not call host networking APIs or depend on host socket state. This evidence supports only the four integer conversions. It says nothing about libSceNet socket, resolver, epoll, offline-state, or error behavior; those imports remain unresolved until their own contracts are established. All sixteen PT_LOAD segments of those eight images have p_align 0x4000 , and in every one p_offset - p_vaddr is exactly 0x4000 . Three guest call sites share one shape: 0x00e04168 , 0x00e04939 and 0x00e05cf9 , each inside functions 0x00e04140 , 0x00e045c0 and 0x00e05a80 . None of them compares the cached value against a constant, and no other function reads it. Inferred, and the premise each inference needs : The ELF ABI takes p_align of a loadable segment to be a multiple of the system page size, and requires p_offset and p_vaddr to be congruent modulo the page size. If the PS4 loader follows both rules for these segments , a page size larger than 0x4000 could not map them at their fixed addresses, while any power-of-two divisor of 0x4000 could. Restricting that to 0x1000 , 0x2000 and 0x4000 adds a second assumption - that the page size is at least 4096 - which is ours, not observed. The guest's own blsr check is consistent with every power of two and selects none of them. So p_align bounds the candidate set under our premises; it does not measure the value the kernel returns, and none of the three candidates is established. Unknown : the number the PS4 reports. Stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096 ( PAGE_SHIFT 12 , sys/amd64/include/param.h ), and Sony's open-source page confirms a FreeBSD kernel but publishes the upstream sources rather than the console's modifications, so that value describes the ancestor and not the target. Each source below establishes a different part: What the call does: POSIX pthread_attr_setdetachstate . A thread created with the attribute starts detached for PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED and joinable for PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE . Invalid detach state: POSIX and FreeBSD's pthread_attr(3) both make any other value EINVAL . Invalid attribute variable: POSIX leaves a null or uninitialised attribute undefined and only recommends EINVAL , and the FreeBSD manual lists no error for it. The behaviour comes from FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_attr_setdetachstate ( lib/libthr/thread/thr_attr.c ), which returns EINVAL when the variable is null or holds no attribute object. The numbers: FreeBSD's <pthread.h> defines the two states as 0 and 1 . The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK header ( include/orbis/_types/pthread.h ) defines ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE and ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED with the same values. That header follows FreeBSD's text, so it corroborates the numbers rather than measuring them independently. As with the mutex functions ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ), the SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number, and the POSIX name returns the number itself. Still open: the detach state a fresh attribute starts with, and the one scePthreadAttrGet copies from a running thread. Both are values the system supplies. POSIX makes joinable the default, but nothing we can cite confirms what the PS4 reports. In FreeBSD libthr, _pthread_create ( thr_create.c ) uses that same default ( _pthread_attr_default ) when it is given no attribute variable or an empty one. The runtime treats both cases as the unknown default, so the outcome, a fatal, does not depend on the PS4 matching libthr there. How the runtime keeps that open: The attribute records a state only when one is set ( has_detach_state ). scePthreadAttrGet replaces the whole attribute, as libthr's pthread_attr_get_np does, so a state set before the copy is dropped. By convention, thread creation reads the state through rt_thread_attr_detach_state ( runtime/include/runtime/process.h ) and never from the field. A fresh attribute's field holds zero, which is the joinable value, so reading the field directly would assume joinable silently. For no variable, an empty variable, or a state nobody set, the reader stops the process ( rt_fatal ), names the call that asked, and says which of those cases it hit. It sets the stack size: the caller's size, or 64 KiB by default. If that is refused, it retries with 16 KiB and reports a fatal error if that fails too. It sets detach state 0 and scheduling policy 1. It creates the thread with (&thread, &attr, entry, argument, name) , comparing a failure with EPERM, EINVAL and EAGAIN as SCE codes. It destroys the attribute and sets the new thread's affinity to a mask of the six bits 0x3f . What the runtime does: scePthreadAttrSetstacksize and pthread_attr_setstacksize record the size. The stack's address is left to the system, as libthr keeps one address and size per attribute. Sizes below 16 KiB are refused with EINVAL. libthr refuses sizes below its minimum that way, and the executable's wrapper names the PS4 's minimum: its callers pass smaller sizes, and when one is refused it asks again for exactly 16 KiB ( 0x02a3b383 ). scePthreadAttrSetschedpolicy records one of FreeBSD's three policies (FIFO 1, OTHER 2, RR 3). libthr refuses any other with ENOTSUP, whose SCE value is not established, so another policy stops by name. A missing attribute answers EINVAL (as an SCE code under the SCE names).
