It gets its own TLS block, a copy of the executable's template as the main thread's is, and its thread pointer goes in GS. It is registered, so scePthreadSelf answers the new thread's handle. entry(argument) is called with the guest's convention. A return ends the thread (POSIX). The attribute's detach state decides whether the host thread is joinable. The scheduling policy is recorded, but the host schedules the thread: guest priorities are not modelled. What stops by name: - no attribute, or no stack size or detach state on it (the PS4 defaults are not established); - a stack address the guest supplies; - the error values. scePthreadSetaffinity records the CPU mask. The executable sets it once per thread, within 0x3f . Scheduling is left to the host, because the host's CPUs say nothing about the PS4 's. An empty mask stops by name. Stops on other threads. A worker thread can fault or reach an unimplemented import. The boot records the first such stop and wakes the main thread ( SIGUSR1 ) to make the usual report. Workers leave the timeout and that signal to the main thread. A local boot with the affinity probe and the rwlocks let through (not committed) reaches the threads milestone and stops next at sceUserServiceInitialize . The user service's start-up calls ( libSceUserService , issue #36) eboot imports sceUserServiceInitialize , sceUserServiceTerminate , sceUserServiceGetInitialUser and sceUserServiceGetLoginUserIdList , among others. The shapes match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's UserService.h and _types/user.h (supporting evidence only): - the parameter block holds a uint32_t priority; - the login list is four user ids, an unused slot holding -1; - id 0xFF is the system's. The executable initializes the service twice: - once at 0x024e1e69 , with priority 0x2bc ; - again at 0x010ba1ac , where it accepts success or exactly 0x80960003 . So a second initialize answers 0x80960003 , the "already initialized" code. What the runtime does. It models one user, the person running it, logged in from the start: - GetInitialUser answers that user's id; - the login list holds it, then three -1 slots; - the id is a handle the runtime hands out, never -1 or 0xFF , because the PS4 's ids are the system's and a title only passes them back. What stops by name: a call before initialize, a missing argument, and the other error values. sceUserServiceGetUserName and sceUserServiceGetEvent stay unbound until the boot reaches them. A local boot (affinity probe and rwlocks let through, not committed) stops next at sceCommonDialogInitialize . The common dialog's initialize ( libSceCommonDialog , issue #40) sceCommonDialogInitialize is the only call eboot imports from libSceCommonDialog . It takes no arguments (OpenOrbis CommonDialog.h , as supporting evidence). The executable calls it twice: - at 0x024e1e8c , logging a failure; - at 0x02023fbb , accepting success or exactly 0x80b80002 . So the first call succeeds and a repeat answers 0x80b80002 , the "already initialized" code. No dialog is shown: each dialog library's own calls do that, and none is provided yet. System settings ( sceSystemServiceParamGetInt , issue #40) sceSystemServiceParamGetInt(id, int32_t *value) reads a console system setting. The setting ids and the language codes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's _types/sys_service.h (id 1 is the language, and 1 there is English (United States)). All nine of the executable's call sites ask for id 1, into a variable preset to -1. They accept codes 0–20 and fall back to a default otherwise. What the runtime does. A setting is the console owner's choice, so the runtime answers what the person running it chose: - tools/boot.py passes --system-param ID=VALUE ; - it defaults the language to 1 (English, United States); - --system-param 1=18 , for example, chooses English (United Kingdom). What stops by name: a setting nobody gave a value, and a missing variable. Content restriction ( sceNpSetContentRestriction , issue #41) The executable's only call, at 0x023b704f , passes a parameter block it built on its stack (an age from a table and a pointer to a restriction list), and it discards the result. The call tells the system which online content the title restricts. The offline runtime offers no online content, so there is nothing to record and it answers 0. A missing block stops by name. Thread variables fit in 40 bits (issue #34) The executable keeps a thread variable's value in 40 bits. Its lock at 0x024368c0 records the owner as scePthreadSelf() masked with 0xffffffffff , then compares that with the whole answer. A thread object above 2^40 would never own a lock it had just taken, and would wait on itself (a local boot hung there). The host heap lies above 2^40, so the runtime allocates thread objects, the main thread's included, from a range it reserves below it, at 0xf000000000 . Flexible memory ( sceKernelMapFlexibleMemory , issue #34) sceKernelMapFlexibleMemory(void **address, size_t length, int32_t protection, int32_t flags) maps memory the system provides without a range of the direct memory pool. The signature is corroborated by the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h . The executable's only call, at 0x02481dbe : - presets the address to 0; - rounds the length up to 16 KiB; - passes protection 3 or 0x33 and flags 0; - on success, requires a non-null address. What the runtime does. It maps fresh zeroed host memory at an address it picks, with the CPU bits of the protection; GPU access is accepted, as for direct memory. The PS4 limits a title's flexible memory to a budget. The budget is not established and the runtime does not enforce it. What stops by name: - an address hint; - map flags; - other protection bits; - a length that is not whole 16 KiB pages; - a missing variable. Network library start-up ( sceNetInit , sceNetTerm , sceNetPoolCreate , issue #41) The names and argument shapes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Net.h , which declares sceNetTerm as returning nothing; the executable reads its result. The behaviour comes from the executable's own calls: - sceNetInit . Seven subsystems each call it once, behind a flag of their own. One ( 0x011c7992 ) accepts success or exactly 0x80410110 , and then does not terminate the library itself. So a repeat initialize answers 0x80410110 , "already initialized". - sceNetTerm . Its callers ( 0x011c79d9 ) accept 0 or exactly 0x804101c8 . Which condition gives the second is not established, so terminating a library that is not initialized stops by name. - sceNetPoolCreate . Every call passes a name and flags 0, treats a negative result as failure, and keeps the result as a pool id it passes on. The runtime hands out ids from 1. The runtime is offline: initializing touches no network. A pool before initialize, without a name or size, or with flags stops by name. SSL and HTTP library start-up ( sceSslInit , sceHttpInit , issue #41) sceSslInit(size_t pool_size) and sceHttpInit(int32_t pool, int32_t ssl, size_t pool_size) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Ssl.h and Http.h declare them. The executable's HTTP manager ( 0x013d1fc0 and 0x013d2050 ): - creates a network pool; - then calls sceSslInit with a size; - then calls sceHttpInit with the pool id, the SSL result and the same size. It treats a negative result as failure, keeps each non-negative one as an id, and passes each id back on teardown. So each call answers a context id; offline, a context is only an id. What stops by name: an id the runtime did not hand out, and a size of 0. HTTP templates ( sceHttpCreateTemplate , sceHttpSetNonblock , issue #41) sceHttpCreateTemplate(int32_t context, const char *user_agent, int32_t version, int32_t proxy) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Http.h declares it. Its version list has 1 for HTTP/1.0 and 2 for HTTP/1.1. The executable's only call ( 0x013d1d32 ) passes the HTTP context id, its user agent string, version 2 and proxy 1. It keeps the result as a template id and passes it straight to the next HTTP call. Offline, a template is only an id. What stops by name: - a context the runtime did not hand out; - no user agent; - a version other than HTTP/1.0 or 1.1; - a proxy value other than the observed 1 (its meaning is not public). sceHttpSetNonblock(id, enable) comes next. OpenOrbis names it without a signature, so its shape comes from the executable's only call ( 0x013d1d41 ): the new template id and 1, with the result discarded. The runtime records the choice and answers 0; offline, nothing ever blocks on a network. An unknown id, and a value other than 0 or 1, stop by name. HTTP waiting handles ( sceHttpCreateEpoll , issue #41) OpenOrbis names sceHttpCreateEpoll without a signature, so its shape comes from the executable's only use, a tail call at 0x013d1d82 . It passes the HTTP context id and the address of an eight-byte slot preset to 0, and its caller ( 0x023e4567 ) discards the result. A handle is an object the library allocates and the title only passes back, so the runtime allocates one per call and answers 0. What the title later does with it (waiting on requests) belongs to other calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: an HTTP context the runtime did not hand out, and a missing slot. HTTP request headers ( sceHttpAddRequestHeader , issue #41) sceHttpAddRequestHeader(id, name, value, mode) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Http.h declares it. The executable's only call ( 0x013d1ed5 ) adds a header to its template with mode 0, and treats only 0 as success. A header only matters to a request the library sends. Offline, no request is ever sent, because every sending call stops by name. So the runtime checks the arguments and answers 0 without keeping the header. What stops by name: - an id that is not one of the runtime 's templates; - a missing name or value; - a mode other than the observed 0 (the modes are not public). Signal masks ( _sigprocmask , issue #34) _sigprocmask(how, set, old) is FreeBSD's sigprocmask(2) : the calling thread's blocked signals. A FreeBSD sigset_t is four 32-bit words, with signal n at bit n - 1. how is SIG_BLOCK (1), SIG_UNBLOCK (2) or SIG_SETMASK (3), and is ignored when there is no new set. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can never be blocked, and are dropped silently. The bundled libc's setjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fcb0 ) reads the mask with SIG_BLOCK and no new set, and its longjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fd00 ) puts it back with SIG_SETMASK . What the runtime does. No signal is delivered to the guest yet. So the runtime keeps each guest thread's mask, a new thread starting with its creator's, and does not apply it to the host thread. What stops by name: an unknown how . Its error is reported through the guest's errno , which the runtime does not model. Thread priorities ( scePthreadGetprio , scePthreadSetprio , issue #34) scePthreadGetprio(thread, int32_t *priority) and scePthreadSetprio(thread, priority) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares them. What the executable does. Its only reader ( 0x02a3b59d ) reads the current priority before choosing a new one from a class. It sets priorities from 256 ( 0x100 ) to 767 ( 0x2ff ), at 0x02a3b63d and 0x0111ab46 . Where a thread's priority comes from: - The main thread. An executable may declare its main thread's settings in its process parameters ( sceUserMainThreadPriority and the like, which homebrew titles define). Without them the main thread runs at SCE_KERNEL_PRIO_FIFO_DEFAULT , 700 (libretro's public ps4_defines.h ). The executable passes the same 700 ( 0x2bc ) as a priority to sceUserServiceInitialize . - This executable's block holds no main thread settings: after relocation only the C library's parameter pointer ( +0x38 ) is set, and +0x18 to +0x37 are empty. - Created threads. A thread created without explicit scheduling inherits its creator's priority (FreeBSD libthr's default attribute, PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED ). The executable sets none. What the runtime does. It records priorities. The host schedules the threads, so priorities change nothing else. What stops by name: - main thread settings in the process parameters (which slot is the priority is not established); - a priority outside 256–767; - a missing thread or variable. clock_gettime and sceKernelClockGettime (libkernel, issue #34) clock_gettime(clockid_t id, struct timespec *tp) is POSIX, with FreeBSD's clock numbers and amd64 struct timespec (two 64-bit fields, seconds and nanoseconds). The bundled libc's time() ( libc.elf+0x2f030 ) asks for clock 13 and returns its seconds. Clock 13 is FreeBSD's CLOCK_SECOND , which FreeBSD answers with the wall clock's whole seconds and 0 nanoseconds ( kern_clock_gettime ). What the runtime does. It answers the clocks whose meaning FreeBSD fixes and the host has: - CLOCK_REALTIME (0) and CLOCK_SECOND (13), from the host's wall clock; - CLOCK_MONOTONIC (4), from the host's monotonic clock. What stops by name: other clocks and a missing timespec. Their errors go through errno , which the runtime does not model. sceKernelClockGettime(id, tp) is the same call under its SCE name. It returns 0x80020000 plus the error number: EINVAL for another clock and EFAULT for a missing timespec, as FreeBSD answers them. The executable's call ( 0x0111a815 ) asks for clock 4, and treats anything but 0 as failure. Process time ( sceKernelGetProcessTime , issue #34) uint64_t sceKernelGetProcessTime(void) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares it, is the time since the process started. Its unit is microseconds. The executable turns it into seconds by dividing by 1,000,000: - at 0x00e4fb6e , through the compiler's multiply by 0x431bde83 and shift by 50; - at 0x0252607e , through a division by the double 1000000.0. It also seeds a random generator with it ( 0x00835dba ). What the runtime does. It measures from its own start, on the host's monotonic clock. Audio job manager start-up ( sceAjmInitialize , sceAjmModuleRegister , issue #37) The audio job manager (libSceAjm) decodes compressed audio in batches of jobs. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Ajm.h names these two calls without signatures, so their shapes come from the executable's only calls: - 0x01118a65 : runs while its context variable still holds -1, and passes 0 and the variable's address. A nonzero result is failure. - 0x01118a81 : then passes that context, 1 and 0, and again treats nonzero as failure. What the runtime does. It hands out a context id and records the registered module. Decoding belongs to the batch and instance calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: - a nonzero first argument to initialize; - a module other than the observed 1 (which codec it names is not public); - a nonzero third argument; - a context the runtime did not hand out; - registering a module twice. Audio output ( sceAudioOutInit , sceAudioOutOpen , sceAudioOutSetVolume , sceAudioOutOutput , issue #37) The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's AudioOut.h declares int32_t sceAudioOutInit(void) and int32_t sceAudioOutOpen(user, port type, index, length, sample rate, param) . Its _types headers give: - port type 0 (main); - format 4 (float stereo); - the error codes 0x8026000E (already initialized) and 0x8026000F (not initialized). What the executable does: - Its only init call ( 0x0111b665 ) accepts success or exactly 0x8026000E . - Its only open ( 0x0111b69d ) passes user 0xff (the system user in the SDK's user types), the main port, index 0, 256 samples, 48000 Hz and a format. It keeps a non-negative result as the port handle. - The format is the executable's own evidence. Its output callback ( 0x0111b600 ) accepts 2 or 8 channels and passes 4 | (channels == 8) . So 4 is float stereo (as in the SDK) and 5 is float with eight channels. The boot opens eight channels. - A second open ( 0x0111b6fc ) passes port type 1 with the same settings, and does not check the result. The PS4 name of type 1 is not public; the sibling Vita SDK calls it BGM. What the runtime does. It records each open port and hands out handles from 1. Sound output belongs to the output calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: any open other than the observed ones, and running out of handles. int32_t sceAudioOutSetVolume(handle, flag, int32_t *volume) , as the SDK declares it, comes next. The executable's only call ( 0x0111b6d6 ) passes its new port, flag 0xff and eight volumes of 32768, and treats nonzero as failure. Flag bit n selects channel n, whose volume is volume[n] . What the runtime does. It records the volumes. What stops by name: - a handle it did not hand out; - a flag naming a channel the port does not have; - a missing array; - a volume outside 0–32768. int32_t sceAudioOutOutput(handle, const void *samples) , as the SDK declares it, hands a port sound. The executable's audio thread ( 0x0111b93c ) hands its port one block at a time ( length samples for every channel). It advances its ring buffer when the result is not negative, and loops with no wait of its own. So the call itself paces the thread: it returns once the port has room for the next block. What the runtime does. It plays nothing yet. - Each port takes one block per length / rate seconds (256 samples at 48000 Hz: 5.33 ms). - A call waits until the block before it would have finished playing, then answers 0 (the caller only checks the sign). - A port that falls behind starts again from now. What stops by name: a missing block, and a handle the runtime did not hand out. Attribute priority and CPU mask ( scePthreadAttrSetschedparam , scePthreadAttrSetaffinity , issue #34) scePthreadAttrSetschedparam(attr, const struct sched_param *param) sets the priority ( sched_param 's one int) of a thread created with the attribute. OpenOrbis' libkernel.h gives the shape; libthr's _pthread_attr_setschedparam gives the semantics. What the executable does. Its thread wrapper ( 0x0111aafd ) sets it without explicit-scheduling inheritance. So under libthr's default ( PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED ), the new thread still starts at its creator's priority. The wrapper then sets the priority itself with scePthreadSetprio ( 0x0111ab46 ). What the runtime does. It records the priority on the attribute. A variable holding no attribute is EINVAL (libthr). What stops by name: a missing param, and a priority outside 256–767. scePthreadAttrSetaffinity(attr, uint64_t mask) is the wrapper's next call ( 0x0111ab0e ), with the CPU mask its caller chose. As for scePthreadSetaffinity , the runtime records the mask (the created thread takes it) and the host schedules. An empty mask stops by name, and a variable holding no attribute is EINVAL . The title's files: /app0 , sceKernelStat , opening and reading (issue #35) The title reads its own data under /app0 , the console's read-only mount of its package. The runtime serves /app0 from your own copy and never writes to it: - tools/boot.py --app0 DIR chooses the copy, defaulting to $BB_APP0 , then $BB_DATA_ROOT/merged . - pbboot takes it as --app0 . - A path under any other mount, and one with a .. component (which could leave the copy), stops by name. sceKernelStat(path, struct stat *) is FreeBSD's stat(2) under its SCE name, which returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. The PS4 's struct stat is FreeBSD 9's amd64 layout, 120 bytes (OpenOrbis' _types/kernel.h , OrbisKernelStat ). What the executable does. Its call at 0x02474519 asks whether /app0/dvdroot_ps4/sound/sprj_mixer.fev exists: - 0 means yes; - exactly 0x80020002 ( ENOENT ) means no; - anything else goes to its error path. What the runtime does. It fills the structure from the host file: - type, size, block count and size, link count and times; - the permission bits without write (the mount is read-only); - device and inode numbers as the host's (they only identify the file); - the birth time as the modification time (the host's stat has none); - owner, group, flags and generation 0. Errors. A missing file answers ENOENT , and a missing directory component ENOTDIR (the same numbers on FreeBSD and Linux). Any other host error stops by name. Opening and reading sceKernelOpen , sceKernelRead , sceKernelPread , sceKernelLseek , sceKernelFstat and sceKernelClose are FreeBSD's open(2) , read(2) , pread(2) , lseek(2) , fstat(2) and close(2) under their SCE names. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares the shapes. Each returns a result, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. The executable opens its data with flags 0 ( O_RDONLY ) and mode 0555. What the runtime does: - Opening. It opens the host file read-only. A request to write, create, truncate or append answers EROFS , as FreeBSD does on a read-only mount. The lookup comes first: a missing file without O_CREAT is ENOENT . Other flag bits stop by name. - Descriptors. A descriptor is the runtime 's own number, from 3 up, standing for a host descriptor (the title only passes it back). One the runtime did not hand out is EBADF . - Seeking. A whence other than 0, 1 or 2 ( SEEK_SET , SEEK_CUR , SEEK_END , the same on FreeBSD and Linux), and a seek before the start, are EINVAL . Implementation rule Implement the established contract and test the RT_SYSLIB entry through its library and symbol name. Keep target-specific values separate from host values. When an argument, ID, return value, or error case is unknown, fail loudly with the call name and leave the question open; never choose a value to make tools/boot.py advance. References POSIX clock_gettime and clock definitions POSIX getpid Older POSIX gettimeofday specification FreeBSD getpagesize(3) ELF ABI, program headers and p_align (loadable segments must be congruent modulo the page size; p_align is the alignment the loader honors) FreeBSD AMD64 param.h (stock PAGE_SIZE 4096) and Sony's open-source page for the PS4 FreeBSD clock_gettime(2) and gettimeofday(2) Linux getpagesize(2) , getpid(2) , clock_gettime(2) , and gettimeofday(2) PSP2SDK sceNetHtonl / sceNetHtons / sceNetNtohl / sceNetNtohs declarations FreeBSD htonl(3) / htons(3) / ntohl(3) / ntohs(3) POSIX sched_yield , FreeBSD sched_yield(2) and FreeBSD pthread_yield(3) ; Linux pthread_yield(3) for the int -returning form ISO C (N1570 draft) 7.24.2.1 memcpy and 7.24.6.1 memset FreeBSD usleep(3) and SUSv2 usleep POSIX pthread_rwlock_rdlock , pthread_rwlock_wrlock , pthread_rwlock_unlock , pthread_rwlock_destroy / init ; FreeBSD libthr thr_rwlock.c and thr_private.h ( THR_RWLOCK_DESTROYED ); FreeBSD kernel kern_umtx.c ( do_rw_rdlock , do_rw_wrlock , do_rw_unlock ) LSB Core __stack_chk_fail and FreeBSD libc libc_stack_protector.c ( __stack_chk_fail , __fail ) POSIX pthread_cond_wait , pthread_cond_signal , pthread_cond_destroy / pthread_cond_init ; FreeBSD libthr thr_cond.c , thr_mutex.c ( _mutex_owned , _mutex_cv_unlock ) and thr_private.h ( THR_COND_DESTROYED ) vitasdk/vita-headers psp2/net/netctl.h - PS Vita, a different operating system: shape of the SceNetCtl declarations, never a PS4 value PSP2SDK psp2/net/netctl.h file reference and vitasdk SceNetCtl user group - the same declarations, with no prose describing any return value in this group vitasdk/vita-headers psp2/error.h - 0 on success as the documented SCE-family return convention OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain Sysmodule.h and _types/sysmodule.h - the sceSysmoduleLoadModule , sceSysmoduleIsLoaded and sceSysmoduleUnloadModule declarations and return convention, and the system module ids (after psdevwiki, "Libraries" ) POSIX pthread_attr_setdetachstate - the detach state semantics, the invalid-value error, and the recommended EINVAL for an uninitialised attribute POSIX pthread_self and pthread_attr_init / pthread_attr_destroy FreeBSD pthread_attr(3) , libthr thr_attr.c ( _pthread_attr_setdetachstate , _pthread_attr_get_np ), thr_create.c ( _pthread_create : the default attribute for a null or empty variable) and include/pthread.h ( PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE , PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED ) OpenOrbis include/orbis/_types/pthread.h - the PS4 homebrew SDK's ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_* values, which follow FreeBSD's
