docs.text: The runtime's own detailed notes on each system call: the evidence, the exact behavior and what stops by name. This page is copied from Paleblood's docs/runtime-syscalls.md every time the wiki syncs, so it always matches the code. For the reader-friendly explanation of the same calls, start with Runtime system calls . This page records contracts used to implement small runtime calls in issues #34 and #41 . Public standards and manuals describe portable or platform-specific API behavior; they do not by themselves prove every detail of the PS4 implementation. Keep the distinction below, and leave unresolved behavior unresolved until public documentation, our own reverse engineering, or observed behavior settles it.
docs.title: Runtime call reference

docs.text: The runtime registry distinguishes behavior it implements from diagnostics for behavior that is still unknown. RT_SYSLIB entries are callable implementations and count toward coverage; RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED entries remain callable so a reached import can fail with a useful name, but do not count as implemented or as supplied imports in progress reports. symbols/imports.csv records getpagesize and gettimeofday as imports of eboot from libScePosix ; libc.elf imports clock_gettime , getpagesize , getpid , and gettimeofday from libkernel . Import rows establish that the names are required, not their arguments, return values at every call site, or all clock IDs. The eight hash- verified target images ( eboot.elf and the seven modules, tools/check_target.py ) all state p_align 0x4000 for every PT_LOAD segment, with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000 (the difference is exactly 0x4000 in each; readelf -l prints the headers). The decompiled frame limiter calls gettimeofday with a null timezone argument. A separate verified clock helper calls sceKernelClockGettime with clock ID 4 , named CLOCK_MONOTONIC in that code. This confirms one monotonic clock request in the game; it does not establish every ID passed through the imported clock_gettime wrapper, or that no other ID is used in unexamined code.
docs.title: Evidence in this repository

docs.text: Function Arguments and representation Publicly documented result and errors Evidence and open questions for PS4 getpagesize(void) No arguments. Returns the target's page size in bytes. The numeric value is platform-specific. getpagesize is not in current POSIX; portable code is directed to sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) . Linux and FreeBSD document the byte count; their manuals do not define a general error return for this function. Linux exposes it as a libc interface, not necessarily a dedicated kernel syscall. FreeBSD notes the system page size may differ from the underlying hardware page size. The import is present twice ( eboot from libScePosix , libc.elf from libkernel ), so both library names are registered against one implementation. The target images bound the value but do not pick one: every PT_LOAD of the eight hash- verified ELFs has p_align 0x4000 with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000, and the ELF ABI's congruence rule then limits the system page size to a divisor of 16384 (4096, 8192 or 16384); p_align is the alignment the image requires, not the page size the system reports. Stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096, and Sony's open-source page confirms the FreeBSD kernel is used but publishes the upstream sources, not the console's modifications, so no public source names the PS4 's own value. The runtime entry is therefore registered with RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED , so a boot that reaches it names the call, and it does not count as implemented ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). What would settle it: one observed getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) result on a console, or a guest call site whose page arithmetic shows the granularity the system uses. See the section "getpagesize: observed, inferred, unknown" below; do not hard-code the build host's page size. getpid(void) No arguments. Returns a pid_t naming the calling process. POSIX specifies that it succeeds and has no error return. Linux process IDs are scoped by PID namespaces; other systems have their own process-ID scope and lifecycle rules. The import is present, but this repository does not establish the guest-visible process ID or its scope. Returning the host PID is not justified by the API contract alone. clock_gettime(clock_id, tp) clock_id selects a clock; tp points to a struct timespec . On the POSIX interface, tv_sec is seconds and tv_nsec is nanoseconds in [0, 1,000,000,000) . The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. POSIX uses 0 for success and -1 with errno for failure. An unsupported clock ID is an EINVAL case. Linux and BSD manuals document additional pointer-error details; use the target contract rather than assuming the host's errno mapping. The imported wrapper is present. The verified sceKernelClockGettime call requests ID 4 ( CLOCK_MONOTONIC ). That is evidence for the SCE entry point only, not proof of the libc wrapper's IDs. Other IDs and exact PS4 error and pointer handling remain unresolved. Unknown IDs must not silently return a fabricated time. gettimeofday(tv, tz) tv points to a struct timeval : seconds since the Epoch and microseconds in [0, 1,000,000) . The historical timezone argument is passed as null at the confirmed game call site. The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. The wall clock can jump and is not a monotonic elapsed-time source. Historical POSIX specified a zero return on success and left errors undefined; Linux documents -1 / EFAULT for inaccessible pointers and ignores the timezone argument. POSIX.1-2024 removed the interface. The imported wrapper and game call sites are present; the game passes null for the second argument. Exact target behavior for bad pointers, non-null timezone arguments, and error mapping is not established. Do not silently ignore an error without evidence. sched_yield(void) No arguments. Returns int . POSIX: the calling thread gives up the processor until it is again at the head of its thread list; 0 on success, -1 with errno otherwise, and POSIX defines no error case for it. FreeBSD documents the same call. Imported by libc.elf from libkernel . Implemented: a guest thread runs on a host thread, so the runtime yields the host thread and returns 0 ( runtime/syslib/kernel_thread.c ). A host failure has no FreeBSD error number to report, so it stops by name. Not observable in a unit test: that the host scheduler actually ran another thread. scePthreadYield Asks for the same yield through the thread library. The PS4 -visible signature is not established. FreeBSD's pthread_yield(3) is void ; Linux's is int (always 0 ). No PS4 -specific public source gives the SCE name's declaration. Imported by eboot and libc.elf from libkernel ; no call site in this repository shows whether the caller reads a result. Registered with RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED : the entry stops by name and does not count as implemented. What would settle it: a guest call site showing whether the return register is read after the call, or a PS4 -specific public declaration. Do not assume an int or 0 from the FreeBSD or Linux analogues. memcpy(dest, src, n) , memset(dest, c, n) (libSceLibcInternal) void *memcpy(void *, const void *, size_t) and void *memset(void *, int, size_t) , the ISO C declarations. ISO C 7.24.2.1 and 7.24.6.1: memcpy copies n bytes from src to dest ; memset writes c converted to unsigned char into the first n bytes; both return dest . Overlapping memcpy regions and null pointers are undefined behaviour. Imported by libSceFios2.elf from libSceLibcInternal ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented with the host's own functions, since the standard fixes the whole result and no target-specific value is involved ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not modelled: what the PS4 C library does for the undefined cases; no public source or call site establishes it. sceKernelUsleep(microseconds) (libkernel), usleep(microseconds) (libScePosix) One unsigned 32-bit count of microseconds, returning int . For sceKernelUsleep the guest fixes the shape: the verified call sites in game/frame_timing/frame_limiter.cpp and game/render/swap_chain_present.cpp declare it as int(uint32_t microseconds) , and their cases expect 0 . FreeBSD's useconds_t is 32-bit unsigned. FreeBSD usleep(3) : suspends the thread for the given microseconds, 0 on success, -1 with EINTR if a signal interrupts it. SUSv2 also let usleep fail with EINVAL from 1,000,000 on; FreeBSD and POSIX.1-2008 (which removed usleep ) have no such limit. sceKernelUsleep is imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf , usleep by eboot . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested time and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Open: usleep with 1,000,000 or more, which stops by name because no PS4 -specific source says whether the guest sleeps or gets EINVAL ; and the SCE error, if any, for sceKernelUsleep , which the guest's sites never check. scePthreadRwlockInit(rwlock, attr, name) , scePthreadRwlockDestroy(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockRdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockWrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTryrdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTrywrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockUnlock(rwlock) (libkernel) A pointer to the guest's rwlock variable ( Init also an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); each returns int32_t . No call site in this repository shows these shapes; they come from the public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declarations, supporting evidence for the shapes only, and match FreeBSD's pthread_rwlock_* . POSIX pthread_rwlock_* , as FreeBSD libthr ( thr_rwlock.c ) and the kernel's umtx read-write lock ( kern_umtx.c ) implement it: a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use and a destroyed rwlock holding 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed rwlock; EBUSY from the try forms when the lock is not available; destroying does not check whether the lock is held, and leaves an unused initializer in place; unlocking is EPERM when another thread holds the write lock or when nobody holds the lock, and readers are counted, not named; a thread that locks again while holding the write lock is not given an error, it waits forever (no owner check in do_rw_wrlock or do_rw_rdlock ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. Imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf ( Tryrdlock by libSceFios2.elf only; symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented on a host rwlock that also records the writer and the reader count, which the host does not expose, for the unlock answers ( runtime/syslib/kernel_rwlock.c ). A missing variable answers EINVAL , as the mutex calls do; unlocking a never-used initializer is EPERM , as for the mutex. Stops by name: Rdlock or Wrlock while the caller holds the write lock (the system would wait forever, the host answers EDEADLK ; neither is useful to return), and an attribute object passed to Init (no imported call creates one, so its contents are not established; an empty attribute variable means the defaults, as in libthr). Not part of this entry: scePthreadRwlockTimedrdlock and Timedwrlock (imported by eboot ; only OpenOrbis gives their microsecond timeout, no call site does) and the libScePosix names. __stack_chk_fail(void) (libkernel) No arguments, no result: void __stack_chk_fail(void) , and it never returns (LSB; FreeBSD libc declares it __dead2 ). Compiler-generated code calls it, not application code. LSB Core: the function that called it is aborted with a message that a stack overflow was detected, and the program then exits. FreeBSD libc logs "stack overflow detected; terminated" and ends the process with SIGABRT . Imported by eboot , libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented as a stop by name ( rt_fatal , which aborts): ending the program is the whole guest-visible contract, so the entry counts as implemented ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not covered: the PS4 's own message or crash report, which the guest cannot observe after it ends; and __stack_chk_guard , a separate data import whose PS4 value is not established (an unbound data import gets a zeroed page, runtime/boot.c ). scePthreadCondInit(cond, attr, name) , scePthreadCondDestroy(cond) , scePthreadCondSignal(cond) , scePthreadCondBroadcast(cond) , scePthreadCondWait(cond, mutex) , scePthreadCondTimedwait(cond, mutex, microseconds) (libkernel) Pointers to the guest's cond and mutex variables; each returns int32_t . The guest fixes the wait shapes: the verified game/kernel/condition_wait.cpp declares Wait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex) and Timedwait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex, uint32_t timeout_us) , a relative timeout in microseconds, not POSIX's absolute timespec . The public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declares all six with these shapes ( Init with an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); it is supporting evidence for the shapes only. POSIX pthread_cond_* , as FreeBSD libthr implements it ( thr_cond.c ): a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use; a destroyed cond holds 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed cond; EBUSY to destroy one with waiters; destroying an unused initializer succeeds and leaves it in place; EPERM when the waiter does not own the mutex, for every mutex type, EINVAL when the mutex is destroyed ( _mutex_owned , thr_mutex.c ); ETIMEDOUT when a timed wait expires; a recursive mutex is released completely for the wait and its count restored after ( _mutex_cv_unlock , _mutex_cv_lock ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. scePthreadCondWait and Timedwait are imported by eboot , libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf , the other four by libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf ( symbols/imports.csv ). The guest's call site checks exactly 0x80020001 (EPERM), 0x80020016 (EINVAL) and 0x8002003c (ETIMEDOUT). Implemented on a host cond on the monotonic clock ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ): the timed wait times out once the given microseconds have passed since the call ( 0 : at once). A missing cond or mutex variable answers EINVAL , as the mutex calls do. Stops by name: an attribute object passed to Init (no imported call creates one, so its contents are not established; an empty attribute variable means the defaults, as in libthr). A wait with a recursive mutex releases every level the caller holds and takes them back after, as libthr does: the runtime tracks each recursive mutex's owner and depth, and releases the extra levels itself around the host wait. Not reproduced: the ownership check for normal and adaptive mutexes, which the host does not make; the error-checking default and the recursive type are checked. The libScePosix names pthread_cond_init , _destroy , _signal , _broadcast and _wait (imported by eboot ) are the same calls with errno values: the executable's call at 0x0247e6d7 passes (&cond, NULL) and its caller compares the result with bare error numbers (12, 16, 34, 35). pthread_cond_timedwait is not part of this entry: it takes an absolute timespec whose PS4 layout and clock are not established, so it stays unbound and stops by name. | sceSysmoduleLoadModule(id) , sceSysmoduleIsLoaded(id) , sceSysmoduleUnloadModule(id) | One system module id, a uint16_t ; each returns int32_t , by the public OpenOrbis Sysmodule.h declarations int32_t f(enum OrbisSysModule moduleId) , the enum being uint16_t ( _types/sysmodule.h ). | OpenOrbis documents each as "0 = Success/Valid or Negatives values are error codes"; no public source gives the error values. | Implemented for the modules game/modules.csv lists with action stub : a load marks the module loaded and succeeds without mapping anything, a query of a loaded one answers 0, an unload clears the mark. Everything else stops by name: a module that is not a stub (the runtime cannot load system modules yet), a second load of a loaded stub (whether the system counts loads is not public), and a query or unload of a stub that is not loaded (the "not loaded" error value is not public). See "Module loading at run time" below. |
docs.title: Interfaces and known behavior

docs.text: Observed in our target : the executable imports sceSysmoduleLoadModule , sceSysmoduleIsLoaded and sceSysmoduleUnloadModule from libSceSysmodule ; its shipped file I/O module imports the load and unload calls too. Neither imports sceKernelLoadStartModule or another loader entry ( symbols/imports.csv ), so a module is asked for by its system module id and nothing else. Five of the seven modules the title ships are listed with action stub in game/modules.csv , which records that the executable imports nothing from them; they are not mapped. Documented publicly : the OpenOrbis toolchain's id list ( include/orbis/_types/sysmodule.h , after psdevwiki's "Libraries" page) names the ids of those five: ORBIS_SYSMODULE_FACE 0x0038 , ORBIS_SYSMODULE_SMART 0x0039 , ORBIS_SYSMODULE_S3DCONVERSION 0x0086 , ORBIS_SYSMODULE_HAND 0x0093 and ORBIS_SYSMODULE_HEAD_TRACKER 0x00cb . They are recorded in the sysmodule column of game/modules.csv ; the runtime itself names no module ( tools/check_agnostic.py ): tools/boot.py passes each stub to pbboot as --stub-module ID:NAME , and the run's status ( stub_modules in symbols/boot.json ) says which of them the guest loaded. Inferred : if nothing we map imports from a stub (as game/modules.csv records for the executable), answering the load without mapping the module cannot leave a call unbound; an import it would have satisfied still shows up unbound in symbols/imports.csv and stops the boot by name. Whether the executable's sites check the result beyond success, and which ids they pass, is not yet observed: the boot stops before the first load today. System modules the runtime provides : a module the title does not ship but loads by id (it is part of the system) can be listed with action runtime once the runtime implements the functions the executable imports from it. tools/boot.py passes it like a stub, so a load is reported as done, and its imports bind to the runtime 's entries by name. The first is libSceAppContent ( 0x00b4 in the OpenOrbis id list), below. Unknown : the error values (a module not loaded, an id the system does not know), and whether a second load of a loaded module is counted, ignored or refused. Each is a named fatal until a console measurement or a guest call site settles it.
docs.title: Module loading at run time (libSceSysmodule)

docs.text: An affinity mask identifies the CPUs on which a thread may run. The current startup stop is a query for the main thread's mask. Returning success without the correct output would change the CPU count that the bundled C library stores; it would not implement the query. Observed in the hash-pinned bundled libc.elf : the function at module offset 0x81a80 initializes a thread attribute, obtains the current thread, and copies its attributes. If those operations succeed, its call at libc.elf+0x81ad0 passes the address of that attribute variable in RDI and the address of a zero-initialized eight-byte stack slot in RSI. This is a two-pointer interface, not FreeBSD's three-argument interface with an explicit buffer size. The return site is libc.elf+0x81ad5 , matching the genuine boot diagnostic. The caller does not check the affinity query's return value: after destroying the attribute it reads the slot, counts its set bits across 64 bits, and stores a 32-bit count. This establishes the consumer's memory requirements, not the real query's write width, the actual mask or its complete error contract. The original consumer also ran through the existing harness on nine private constructed fixtures with scripted imports, using each compiler's loader . It produced the expected counts for zero, low-bit, high-bit and all-bit masks, and exercised both earlier failure branches. A scripted nonzero affinity return with a supplied mask still produced that mask's count, corroborating that this caller ignores the return. These are original-consumer observations under synthetic import behavior, not observations of PS4 affinity, recorded gameplay, complete instruction-trace verification or an original-versus-replacement comparison. No function status changes follow from them. Public supporting evidence: the OpenOrbis homebrew header libkernel.h declares a signed 32-bit return and an attribute pointer plus an output pointer. Its comment explicitly leaves the mask type unfinished; the declaration is corroboration, not a measured PS4 contract. The FreeBSD 9.3 affinity manual describes retrieving a stored attribute mask, success/error returns and invalid attributes, but its API includes a size argument absent at this target call. Its errors and CPU-set layout cannot simply be assigned to the SCE interface. Still required before implementation: independently establish the main thread's actual mask, how a fresh attribute differs from one filled by scePthreadAttrGet , the exact output write extent, success/error results, and invalid/null attribute or output handling. Host CPU availability and a guessed console core count establish none of these. No specific affinity implementation is added or registered by this investigation; the import remains unbound. A useful target measurement would record the console/firmware and executable identities, the results of attribute initialization and copying from scePthreadSelf , the getter's return bits, the output bytes with adjacent canaries, and repeated observations without changing affinity. Check current claims in issue #34 before taking implementation work; mentions of the boot blocker are not themselves contributor claims. Generic gameplay capture remains separate contributor-owned work, not a reason to synthesize the missing affinity observation.
docs.title: scePthreadAttrGetaffinity: the startup consumer and missing evidence

docs.text: The only clock ID confirmed by a decompiled game call in this repository is 4 , used with sceKernelClockGettime and identified there as CLOCK_MONOTONIC . This does not prove that the game passes 4 to the imported clock_gettime wrapper. POSIX defines clock identifiers symbolically; their numeric values are implementation-specific. Linux adds clocks such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME ; FreeBSD has its own clock set, including CLOCK_UPTIME variants. Their names and numeric values are not interchangeable evidence for PS4 behavior. CLOCK_MONOTONIC represents elapsed time from an unspecified starting point and is not the wall clock. The precise effects of suspend, rate correction, and resolution vary by implementation. gettimeofday and CLOCK_REALTIME represent wall time tied to the Epoch and can move when system time changes. No source examined here establishes that the game asks the imported clock_gettime wrapper for CLOCK_REALTIME , CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW , CLOCK_BOOTTIME , or another ID.
docs.title: Clock IDs and platform differences

docs.text: The four libSceNet imports sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs take and return 32-bit or 16-bit unsigned integers, respectively. Public PSP2SDK API declarations provide those widths for the SCE names. The standard byte-order contract converts host order to network (big-endian) order for hton* , and reverses that conversion for ntoh* ; this is documented by the FreeBSD byte-order manual . Paleblood's guest ABI is AMD64, so these four conversions are byte reversals. Their implementations do not call host networking APIs or depend on host socket state. This evidence supports only the four integer conversions. It says nothing about libSceNet socket, resolver, epoll, offline-state, or error behavior; those imports remain unresolved until their own contracts are established.
docs.title: Network byte-order helpers

docs.text: The executable imports sceNetInetPton from libSceNet . Target call-site inspection found four unconditional call instructions (at 0x0085785e , 0x011c7a7b , 0x02f984f6 , and 0x02df348d ); each passes address family 2 and supplies the result as an IPv4 address. The consumers use a positive return as success. This establishes Bloodborne's observed call shape, not every address family supported by the PS4 library. The import thunk and pointer-table references are not additional call sites. For the observed AF_INET path, the runtime uses the documented BSD inet_pton(3) contract : parse dotted-decimal IPv4 text into four network-order bytes, return 1 for valid input and 0 for malformed input. This conversion does not open a socket or perform network I/O. Other target address families and null-pointer error behavior remain unresolved, so the runtime emits a named diagnostic for those inputs instead of forwarding host-specific errors.
docs.title: IPv4 text conversion (sceNetInetPton, issue #41)

docs.text: Observed in our target (read-only; the eight images verify against target.sha256 and target.image.sha256 ): symbols/imports.csv has exactly two getpagesize rows - eboot from libScePosix and libc.elf from libkernel . No sysconf and no quad-page call is imported, so this is the only page-size query the guest has. All sixteen PT_LOAD segments of those eight images have p_align 0x4000 , and in every one p_offset - p_vaddr is exactly 0x4000 . Three guest call sites share one shape: 0x00e04168 , 0x00e04939 and 0x00e05cf9 , each inside functions 0x00e04140 , 0x00e045c0 and 0x00e05a80 . Each is a lazy initialiser: a guard tests 0x05859ec0 , the call is made, the result is cltq -extended, blsr %rax,%rcx with jne rejects it unless it is a power of two, and the value is cached in 0x05859ec8 beside three fixed siblings ( 0x10000 , 0x40000 , 0x200000 ). 0x05859ec8 has exactly five cross-references in the executable: the three writes above and two reads, all inside those same three functions. None of them compares the cached value against a constant, and no other function reads it. Inferred, and the premise each inference needs : The ELF ABI takes p_align of a loadable segment to be a multiple of the system page size, and requires p_offset and p_vaddr to be congruent modulo the page size. If the PS4 loader follows both rules for these segments , a page size larger than 0x4000 could not map them at their fixed addresses, while any power-of-two divisor of 0x4000 could. Restricting that to 0x1000 , 0x2000 and 0x4000 adds a second assumption - that the page size is at least 4096 - which is ours, not observed. The guest's own blsr check is consistent with every power of two and selects none of them. So p_align bounds the candidate set under our premises; it does not measure the value the kernel returns, and none of the three candidates is established. Unknown : the number the PS4 reports. Stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096 ( PAGE_SHIFT 12 , sys/amd64/include/param.h ), and Sony's open-source page confirms a FreeBSD kernel but publishes the upstream sources rather than the console's modifications, so that value describes the ancestor and not the target. Our own loader does not depend on a page size either: it copies PT_LOAD segments at byte-exact p_vaddr into one image buffer ( runtime/loader.c , rt_elf_map ) and uses p_align only for TLS, and the 4096 s in runtime/boot.c are host allocation sizes. What would settle it: one observed getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) result on a console.
docs.title: getpagesize: observed, inferred, unknown

docs.text: The executable imports exactly six functions from libSceNetCtl and neither sceNetCtlInit nor sceNetCtlTerm ( symbols/imports.csv ), so the runtime answers the connection queries itself and the game takes its offline paths. The public declarations of the same API family on PS Vita ( psp2/net/netctl.h in vitasdk/vita-headers, and the PSP2SDK header reference) give the shape of the calls: a state query through an int * , an information query by an int module id into a structure pointer, one NAT query through a structure pointer, and a callback check that takes nothing and returns int . Vita is a different operating system, so those declarations are evidence for the shape only and their numbers are never proof of a PS4 value. No value in this group is taken from another runtime 's behaviour: where no public source reaches, the guest's own call sites decide. They have settled the state numbers (0 is not up, 3 is connected) and the callback keying (an id handed back, not a state), and everything they do not reach - error codes, structure layouts, the offline answers - stays a fatal that names the question and the evidence that would close it. Function Arguments and representation Publicly documented result and errors Evidence and open questions for PS4 sceNetCtlGetState(int *state) One pointer to a 32-bit int , by the Vita-era declaration. Writes the state the system is in. The Vita-era family names the disconnected state first in its state enum, so 0 there. Public sources give no error return for a query that succeeds. Implemented: an offline runtime reports the disconnected state and succeeds. The guest fixes the numbers for us - one site tests the returned slot against 0 at 0x00dfd260 to decide whether to keep waiting, another bounds it with cmp $0x3; ja before a four-entry table at 0x020413f3 (so the states it can see are {0, 1, 2, 3}), and equality with 3 is the connected branch at 0x010b839f and in its own callback at 0x010b45e5 . Still open: what 1 and 2 mean, the PS4 enumerator names, and the error value for a null state pointer (fatal). sceNetCtlCheckCallback(void) No arguments; returns int , by the Vita-era declaration. Runs the callbacks made due by a state change. No public source describes the return value at all, only the declaration. Implemented as 0, the one value both candidate contracts give while nothing is due: the runtime never leaves the disconnected state, so no callback runs. Which reading is the PS4 's (a success code, or the number of callbacks it ran)? It only matters once a state change is possible. sceNetCtlRegisterCallback(void *callback, void *arg, int *cid) A callback pointer, an argument pointer and an out-parameter int *cid , returning int . The guest's own call at 0x010b8352 passes a function in the image, this , and lea -0x78(%rbp) , a slot it never writes, then reads that slot back at 0x010b8428 into its object at +0x130 . Vita-era registration is keyed by a callback id the caller receives back ( func, arg, int *cid ); the guest's sites show the same shape on PS4 . The two public Vita-era sources disagree about the callback's return type, so the pointer stays opaque and no signature is modelled for it - the guest's callback at 0x010b45e0 does show it being dispatched as (state, arg). Implemented: each registration gets a fresh id written through the caller's pointer, numbered from 1 so an id can never look like an unwritten slot, and nothing is ever dispatched while offline. Open: the error values for a null callback or a null id slot, the table's capacity, and whether re-registering the same callback replaces or adds (we add, being keyed by id). sceNetCtlUnregisterCallback(int cid) One int : the id a previous register call handed back. The guest passes the field it stored from that out-parameter ( 0x010b8f8d ). The Vita-era form takes the callback id int cid , which the sites match. Implemented for an id we handed out: remove it and succeed. Fatal for an id we never handed out, or one already removed - no public source gives the PS4 answer and the guest's own paths never reach it. sceNetCtlGetInfo(int module, void *info) Claimed as an int module id and a structure pointer, by the Vita-era sceNetCtlInetGetInfo(int code, SceNetCtlInfo *info) . The Vita-era union's members and its size are another operating system's; nothing public describes the PS4 structure. Not implemented: fatal before touching the buffer. The guest narrows the question - every site in the executable passes module id 14 ( 0x00dfd2b1 , 0x020413ee ), each with a buffer in the second argument that it prints as a string on the success path, and no other id appears anywhere. Open: what id 14 means on PS4 , its offline answer, and the structure's size and layout. The fatal names the id, so a boot run reports which ones the guest asks for. sceNetCtlGetNatInfo(void *nat_info) Claimed as one structure pointer, by the Vita-era sceNetCtlGetNatInfo(SceNetCtlNatInfo *natinfo) . The Vita-era structure starts with a size field the caller fills in; the PS4 layout is not public. Not implemented: fatal before writing. The guest's sites bound it - each writes 16 at offset 0 before the call ( 0x01889417 ) and reads back only offset 8 afterwards ( 0x01889436 ). Open: the PS4 meaning of the value at offset 8, the NAT type values, and what a system with no connection reports. The reported size is named in the fatal, so a caller reporting something other than 16 is itself evidence that the layout is not what the sites suggest. 0 is the success value, the convention public SCE-family documentation states for these calls (the @return 0 on success lines in psp2/error.h of vita-headers). libSceNetCtl's own error codes have no public source, so no path in runtime/syslib/netctl.c returns one: a case that would need an error value stops the boot by name instead.
docs.title: Network connection state (libSceNetCtl, issue #41)

docs.text: eboot and libSceFios2.elf import scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate from libkernel , and eboot imports pthread_attr_setdetachstate from libScePosix ( symbols/imports.csv ). Each source below establishes a different part: What the call does: POSIX pthread_attr_setdetachstate . A thread created with the attribute starts detached for PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED and joinable for PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE . Invalid detach state: POSIX and FreeBSD's pthread_attr(3) both make any other value EINVAL . Invalid attribute variable: POSIX leaves a null or uninitialised attribute undefined and only recommends EINVAL , and the FreeBSD manual lists no error for it. The behaviour comes from FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_attr_setdetachstate ( lib/libthr/thread/thr_attr.c ), which returns EINVAL when the variable is null or holds no attribute object. The numbers: FreeBSD's <pthread.h> defines the two states as 0 and 1 . The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK header ( include/orbis/_types/pthread.h ) defines ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE and ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED with the same values. That header follows FreeBSD's text, so it corroborates the numbers rather than measuring them independently. As with the mutex functions ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ), the SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number, and the POSIX name returns the number itself. Still open: the detach state a fresh attribute starts with, and the one scePthreadAttrGet copies from a running thread. Both are values the system supplies. POSIX makes joinable the default, but nothing we can cite confirms what the PS4 reports. In FreeBSD libthr, _pthread_create ( thr_create.c ) uses that same default ( _pthread_attr_default ) when it is given no attribute variable or an empty one. The runtime treats both cases as the unknown default, so the outcome, a fatal, does not depend on the PS4 matching libthr there. How the runtime keeps that open: The attribute records a state only when one is set ( has_detach_state ). scePthreadAttrGet replaces the whole attribute, as libthr's pthread_attr_get_np does, so a state set before the copy is dropped. By convention, thread creation reads the state through rt_thread_attr_detach_state ( runtime/include/runtime/process.h ) and never from the field. A fresh attribute's field holds zero, which is the joinable value, so reading the field directly would assume joinable silently. For no variable, an empty variable, or a state nobody set, the reader stops the process ( rt_fatal ), names the call that asked, and says which of those cases it hit. What would settle it: an observed scePthreadAttrGetdetachstate result on a console, for a fresh attribute and for one filled by scePthreadAttrGet from the main thread. Guest call sites would also settle it: a thread created without a detach state being set, then joined or detached ( scePthreadJoin , pthread_join and scePthreadDetach are imported).
docs.title: Thread attribute detach state (scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports pthread_self , pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy from libScePosix ( symbols/imports.csv ), next to the libkernel SCE names the runtime already implements. They are the same calls with the POSIX error convention, as for the mutex and detach-state calls: pthread_self has no error return (POSIX), so it answers what scePthreadSelf answers: the calling thread's own variable value. With no guest thread registered on the host thread it stops by the name the guest used. pthread_attr_init allocates the attribute object and stores it in the variable; ENOMEM when it cannot (POSIX; FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_attr_init ). pthread_attr_destroy frees it and empties the variable; EINVAL for a missing or empty variable (libthr's _pthread_attr_destroy ). The POSIX names return the error number itself, the SCE names 0x80020000 plus it, and an object made under one name is freed under the other. A missing variable passed to pthread_attr_init is undefined in POSIX and unchecked in libthr. The runtime answers EINVAL under both names, as the SCE name already did; no PS4 source or call site says otherwise.
docs.title: POSIX names of the thread self and attribute calls (libScePosix, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports sceKernelGetDirectMemorySize , sceKernelAllocateDirectMemory , sceKernelMapDirectMemory and sceKernelReleaseDirectMemory ( symbols/imports.csv ). Its first use is the startup heap, at 0x02481a80 : It asks for the size. It allocates 0x7400000 bytes, aligned to 0x200000 , anywhere from 0 to that size, with memory type 0. It maps the range read/write (protection 3) with flags 0, so the system picks the address, at the same alignment. If the map fails, it releases the range. On any failure it logs an error and builds its heap from a null base, so these calls have to succeed. The signatures match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h , as supporting evidence only. The pool. Direct memory is a host memory file. An allocation is a range of it and a map is a host mapping of that range, so two maps of one range see the same bytes. The size. sceKernelGetDirectMemorySize answers the size of that pool (5 GiB), a choice of the runtime . The PS4 's value is not established here. A title that sizes its allocations from the answer sizes them from the runtime 's pool. Allocation. It takes the lowest start at or above the search start that fits before the search end. GPU access. The executable maps with protection 3 and 0x33 , CPU and GPU read/write ( 0x10 and 0x20 in the public SDK list). The runtime has no GPU yet, so the host mapping takes the CPU bits. What stops by name. Every case whose PS4 answer is not established stops with the function's name: lengths, starts or alignments that are not multiples of 16 KiB (the granularity the executable's calls use); memory types other than 0, 3 and 10; map flags, and an address hint without flags; protection other than CPU and GPU read and write; a range that does not fit or was not allocated; releasing part of a range or a mapped one; the error values. Measured with a local boot that let the libc affinity probe return (not committed): with these four calls the executable's heap setup succeeds and the boot reaches entry . It stops next at scePthreadRwlockInit .
docs.title: Direct memory (libkernel, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports sceKernelCreateSema , sceKernelDeleteSema , sceKernelWaitSema , sceKernelSignalSema and sceKernelPollSema ( symbols/imports.csv ). Its own calls are the evidence here. They include the audio wrappers at 0x0111ad10 – 0x0111adc0 and the wrappers at 0x0084ac20 – 0x0084ac83 : Create: (&handle, name, attr, initial, max, NULL) , with attr 1 or 2, initial 0 or passed through, and max 0xffff , 1, or passed through. Wait: (handle, 1, NULL) , with no timeout. Signal: (handle, 1) or a count passed through. Delete: (handle) . Results: every result is compared with 0. The signatures, and attr 1 = FIFO and 2 = priority wake order, match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK headers (supporting evidence only). What the runtime does. A semaphore is a runtime object behind the handle. Wait blocks until the units are there, and waiters are served in the order they arrived. Signal adds units and wakes the waiters. What stops by name. Every case whose PS4 answer is not established stops with the function's name: - timeouts; - a missing semaphore, variable or name; - an option parameter, and attributes other than 1 and 2; - counts outside 0 <= initial <= max ; - signalling past the maximum; - a poll that cannot be satisfied now; - deleting a semaphore with waiters; - a second waiter under priority order (guest thread priorities are not modelled); - a wait for more than one unit behind another waiter (whether it may be passed is not established); - the error values. A local boot that let the affinity probe and the rwlocks through (not committed) stopped next at sceKernelCreateSema . With throwaway answers past it, the next stops were gettimeofday , then sceSysmoduleLoadModule for system module 0x00b4 .
docs.title: Kernel semaphores (libkernel, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports gettimeofday from libScePosix , libc.elf imports it from libkernel , and libSceFios2.elf imports sceKernelGettimeofday ( symbols/imports.csv ). The executable's own call, at 0x024e2703 , passes a timeval on its stack and no timezone, and reads both fields as 64-bit values. That matches FreeBSD's amd64 struct timeval : seconds, then microseconds. The runtime answers the host's wall clock, under all three names, because the guest asks the system it runs on. It returns 0. Given no timeval, the POSIX names fill nothing and succeed, as FreeBSD's sys_gettimeofday does. What stops by name: - a timezone argument (obsolete in POSIX; what the PS4 fills in is not established); - a missing timeval for sceKernelGettimeofday (its error value is not established).
docs.title: Time of day (gettimeofday, sceKernelGettimeofday, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot loads system module 0x00b4 ( libSceAppContent in the OpenOrbis id list). It imports sceAppContentInitialize , sceAppContentAppParamGetInt and sceAppContentGetAddcontInfoList from it. The public toolchain header names these functions but gives no signatures, so the shapes come from the executable's own calls at 0x024261d8 – 0x0242622a : Initialize: sceAppContentInitialize(init, boot) . Both structures are zeroed first and the result is not checked. Parameters: sceAppContentAppParamGetInt(id, int32_t *value) for ids 0 to 4, each into a global, results not checked. Ids 1–4 are the title's USER_DEFINED_PARAM_1 – 4 from its own sce_sys/param.sfo . Id 0 is the SKU flag, which the system answers. Neither the boot parameter's contents, the SKU answer, the answer for a key the file lacks, nor the error values are public. Which answers this executable observes. A scan of every RIP-relative reference shows that the boot parameter and the outputs for ids 0, 2, 3 and 4 are only passed to these calls. Nothing reads them afterwards. Only id 1's output is read (at five sites). How the runtime answers. It answers only what the game's own data declares, in game/app_params.csv : - an id with source sfo gets its value from the user's own parameter file (read by tools/boot.py and passed as --app-param ID=VALUE ); - an id with source unread succeeds without being written; - boot set to unread lets the initialize call pass over the boot parameter. Anything else stops by name: an undeclared id, a boot parameter not declared unread, and a missing value variable. A local boot with the affinity probe and the rwlocks let through (not committed) loads the module, passes these calls, and stops next at pthread_cond_init ( libScePosix ).
docs.title: Application content (libSceAppContent, issue #34)

docs.text: The executable's thread wrapper ( 0x02a3b324 – 0x02a3b46e ) sets up each thread like this: It initializes an attribute. It sets the stack size: the caller's size, or 64 KiB by default. If that is refused, it retries with 16 KiB and reports a fatal error if that fails too. It sets detach state 0 and scheduling policy 1. It creates the thread with (&thread, &attr, entry, argument, name) , comparing a failure with EPERM, EINVAL and EAGAIN as SCE codes. It destroys the attribute and sets the new thread's affinity to a mask of the six bits 0x3f . What the runtime does: scePthreadAttrSetstacksize and pthread_attr_setstacksize record the size. The stack's address is left to the system, as libthr keeps one address and size per attribute. Sizes below 16 KiB are refused with EINVAL. libthr refuses sizes below its minimum that way, and the executable's wrapper names the PS4 's minimum: its callers pass smaller sizes, and when one is refused it asks again for exactly 16 KiB ( 0x02a3b383 ). scePthreadAttrSetschedpolicy records one of FreeBSD's three policies (FIFO 1, OTHER 2, RR 3). libthr refuses any other with ENOTSUP, whose SCE value is not established, so another policy stops by name. A missing attribute answers EINVAL (as an SCE code under the SCE names).
docs.title: Thread attributes: stack size and scheduling policy (issue #34)

docs.text: scePthreadCreate(&thread, &attr, entry, argument, name) runs the guest on a new host thread: The thread gets its own guest stack, of the attribute's size. It gets its own TLS block, a copy of the executable's template as the main thread's is, and its thread pointer goes in GS. It is registered, so scePthreadSelf answers the new thread's handle. entry(argument) is called with the guest's convention. A return ends the thread (POSIX). The attribute's detach state decides whether the host thread is joinable. The scheduling policy is recorded, but the host schedules the thread: guest priorities are not modelled. What stops by name: - no attribute, or no stack size or detach state on it (the PS4 defaults are not established); - a stack address the guest supplies; - the error values. scePthreadSetaffinity records the CPU mask. The executable sets it once per thread, within 0x3f . Scheduling is left to the host, because the host's CPUs say nothing about the PS4 's. An empty mask stops by name. Stops on other threads. A worker thread can fault or reach an unimplemented import. The boot records the first such stop and wakes the main thread ( SIGUSR1 ) to make the usual report. Workers leave the timeout and that signal to the main thread. A local boot with the affinity probe and the rwlocks let through (not committed) reaches the threads milestone and stops next at sceUserServiceInitialize .
docs.title: Thread creation (scePthreadCreate, scePthreadSetaffinity, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports sceUserServiceInitialize , sceUserServiceTerminate , sceUserServiceGetInitialUser and sceUserServiceGetLoginUserIdList , among others. The shapes match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's UserService.h and _types/user.h (supporting evidence only): - the parameter block holds a uint32_t priority; - the login list is four user ids, an unused slot holding -1; - id 0xFF is the system's. The executable initializes the service twice: - once at 0x024e1e69 , with priority 0x2bc ; - again at 0x010ba1ac , where it accepts success or exactly 0x80960003 . So a second initialize answers 0x80960003 , the "already initialized" code. What the runtime does. It models one user, the person running it, logged in from the start: - GetInitialUser answers that user's id; - the login list holds it, then three -1 slots; - the id is a handle the runtime hands out, never -1 or 0xFF , because the PS4 's ids are the system's and a title only passes them back. What stops by name: a call before initialize, a missing argument, and the other error values. sceUserServiceGetUserName and sceUserServiceGetEvent stay unbound until the boot reaches them. A local boot (affinity probe and rwlocks let through, not committed) stops next at sceCommonDialogInitialize .
docs.title: The user service's start-up calls (libSceUserService, issue #36)

docs.text: sceCommonDialogInitialize is the only call eboot imports from libSceCommonDialog . It takes no arguments (OpenOrbis CommonDialog.h , as supporting evidence). The executable calls it twice: - at 0x024e1e8c , logging a failure; - at 0x02023fbb , accepting success or exactly 0x80b80002 . So the first call succeeds and a repeat answers 0x80b80002 , the "already initialized" code. No dialog is shown: each dialog library's own calls do that, and none is provided yet.
docs.title: The common dialog's initialize (libSceCommonDialog, issue #40)

docs.text: sceSystemServiceParamGetInt(id, int32_t *value) reads a console system setting. The setting ids and the language codes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's _types/sys_service.h (id 1 is the language, and 1 there is English (United States)). All nine of the executable's call sites ask for id 1, into a variable preset to -1. They accept codes 0–20 and fall back to a default otherwise. What the runtime does. A setting is the console owner's choice, so the runtime answers what the person running it chose: - tools/boot.py passes --system-param ID=VALUE ; - it defaults the language to 1 (English, United States); - --system-param 1=18 , for example, chooses English (United Kingdom). What stops by name: a setting nobody gave a value, and a missing variable.
docs.title: System settings (sceSystemServiceParamGetInt, issue #40)

docs.text: The executable's only call, at 0x023b704f , passes a parameter block it built on its stack (an age from a table and a pointer to a restriction list), and it discards the result. The call tells the system which online content the title restricts. The offline runtime offers no online content, so there is nothing to record and it answers 0. A missing block stops by name.
docs.title: Content restriction (sceNpSetContentRestriction, issue #41)

docs.text: The executable keeps a thread variable's value in 40 bits. Its lock at 0x024368c0 records the owner as scePthreadSelf() masked with 0xffffffffff , then compares that with the whole answer. A thread object above 2^40 would never own a lock it had just taken, and would wait on itself (a local boot hung there). The host heap lies above 2^40, so the runtime allocates thread objects, the main thread's included, from a range it reserves below it, at 0xf000000000 .
docs.title: Thread variables fit in 40 bits (issue #34)

docs.text: sceKernelMapFlexibleMemory(void **address, size_t length, int32_t protection, int32_t flags) maps memory the system provides without a range of the direct memory pool. The signature is corroborated by the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h . The executable's only call, at 0x02481dbe : - presets the address to 0; - rounds the length up to 16 KiB; - passes protection 3 or 0x33 and flags 0; - on success, requires a non-null address. What the runtime does. It maps fresh zeroed host memory at an address it picks, with the CPU bits of the protection; GPU access is accepted, as for direct memory. The PS4 limits a title's flexible memory to a budget. The budget is not established and the runtime does not enforce it. What stops by name: - an address hint; - map flags; - other protection bits; - a length that is not whole 16 KiB pages; - a missing variable.
docs.title: Flexible memory (sceKernelMapFlexibleMemory, issue #34)

docs.text: The names and argument shapes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Net.h , which declares sceNetTerm as returning nothing; the executable reads its result. The behaviour comes from the executable's own calls: - sceNetInit . Seven subsystems each call it once, behind a flag of their own. One ( 0x011c7992 ) accepts success or exactly 0x80410110 , and then does not terminate the library itself. So a repeat initialize answers 0x80410110 , "already initialized". - sceNetTerm . Its callers ( 0x011c79d9 ) accept 0 or exactly 0x804101c8 . Which condition gives the second is not established, so terminating a library that is not initialized stops by name. - sceNetPoolCreate . Every call passes a name and flags 0, treats a negative result as failure, and keeps the result as a pool id it passes on. The runtime hands out ids from 1. The runtime is offline: initializing touches no network. A pool before initialize, without a name or size, or with flags stops by name.
docs.title: Network library start-up (sceNetInit, sceNetTerm, sceNetPoolCreate, issue #41)

docs.text: sceSslInit(size_t pool_size) and sceHttpInit(int32_t pool, int32_t ssl, size_t pool_size) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Ssl.h and Http.h declare them. The executable's HTTP manager ( 0x013d1fc0 and 0x013d2050 ): - creates a network pool; - then calls sceSslInit with a size; - then calls sceHttpInit with the pool id, the SSL result and the same size. It treats a negative result as failure, keeps each non-negative one as an id, and passes each id back on teardown. So each call answers a context id; offline, a context is only an id. What stops by name: an id the runtime did not hand out, and a size of 0.
docs.title: SSL and HTTP library start-up (sceSslInit, sceHttpInit, issue #41)

docs.text: sceHttpCreateTemplate(int32_t context, const char *user_agent, int32_t version, int32_t proxy) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Http.h declares it. Its version list has 1 for HTTP/1.0 and 2 for HTTP/1.1. The executable's only call ( 0x013d1d32 ) passes the HTTP context id, its user agent string, version 2 and proxy 1. It keeps the result as a template id and passes it straight to the next HTTP call. Offline, a template is only an id. What stops by name: - a context the runtime did not hand out; - no user agent; - a version other than HTTP/1.0 or 1.1; - a proxy value other than the observed 1 (its meaning is not public). sceHttpSetNonblock(id, enable) comes next. OpenOrbis names it without a signature, so its shape comes from the executable's only call ( 0x013d1d41 ): the new template id and 1, with the result discarded. The runtime records the choice and answers 0; offline, nothing ever blocks on a network. An unknown id, and a value other than 0 or 1, stop by name.
docs.title: HTTP templates (sceHttpCreateTemplate, sceHttpSetNonblock, issue #41)

docs.text: OpenOrbis names sceHttpCreateEpoll without a signature, so its shape comes from the executable's only use, a tail call at 0x013d1d82 . It passes the HTTP context id and the address of an eight-byte slot preset to 0, and its caller ( 0x023e4567 ) discards the result. A handle is an object the library allocates and the title only passes back, so the runtime allocates one per call and answers 0. What the title later does with it (waiting on requests) belongs to other calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: an HTTP context the runtime did not hand out, and a missing slot.
docs.title: HTTP waiting handles (sceHttpCreateEpoll, issue #41)

docs.text: sceHttpAddRequestHeader(id, name, value, mode) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Http.h declares it. The executable's only call ( 0x013d1ed5 ) adds a header to its template with mode 0, and treats only 0 as success. A header only matters to a request the library sends. Offline, no request is ever sent, because every sending call stops by name. So the runtime checks the arguments and answers 0 without keeping the header. What stops by name: - an id that is not one of the runtime 's templates; - a missing name or value; - a mode other than the observed 0 (the modes are not public).
docs.title: HTTP request headers (sceHttpAddRequestHeader, issue #41)

docs.text: _sigprocmask(how, set, old) is FreeBSD's sigprocmask(2) : the calling thread's blocked signals. A FreeBSD sigset_t is four 32-bit words, with signal n at bit n - 1. how is SIG_BLOCK (1), SIG_UNBLOCK (2) or SIG_SETMASK (3), and is ignored when there is no new set. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can never be blocked, and are dropped silently. The bundled libc's setjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fcb0 ) reads the mask with SIG_BLOCK and no new set, and its longjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fd00 ) puts it back with SIG_SETMASK . What the runtime does. No signal is delivered to the guest yet. So the runtime keeps each guest thread's mask, a new thread starting with its creator's, and does not apply it to the host thread. What stops by name: an unknown how . Its error is reported through the guest's errno , which the runtime does not model.
docs.title: Signal masks (_sigprocmask, issue #34)

docs.text: scePthreadGetprio(thread, int32_t *priority) and scePthreadSetprio(thread, priority) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares them. What the executable does. Its only reader ( 0x02a3b59d ) reads the current priority before choosing a new one from a class. It sets priorities from 256 ( 0x100 ) to 767 ( 0x2ff ), at 0x02a3b63d and 0x0111ab46 . Where a thread's priority comes from: - The main thread. An executable may declare its main thread's settings in its process parameters ( sceUserMainThreadPriority and the like, which homebrew titles define). Without them the main thread runs at SCE_KERNEL_PRIO_FIFO_DEFAULT , 700 (libretro's public ps4_defines.h ). The executable passes the same 700 ( 0x2bc ) as a priority to sceUserServiceInitialize . - This executable's block holds no main thread settings: after relocation only the C library's parameter pointer ( +0x38 ) is set, and +0x18 to +0x37 are empty. - Created threads. A thread created without explicit scheduling inherits its creator's priority (FreeBSD libthr's default attribute, PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED ). The executable sets none. What the runtime does. It records priorities. The host schedules the threads, so priorities change nothing else. What stops by name: - main thread settings in the process parameters (which slot is the priority is not established); - a priority outside 256–767; - a missing thread or variable.
docs.title: Thread priorities (scePthreadGetprio, scePthreadSetprio, issue #34)

docs.text: clock_gettime(clockid_t id, struct timespec *tp) is POSIX, with FreeBSD's clock numbers and amd64 struct timespec (two 64-bit fields, seconds and nanoseconds). The bundled libc's time() ( libc.elf+0x2f030 ) asks for clock 13 and returns its seconds. Clock 13 is FreeBSD's CLOCK_SECOND , which FreeBSD answers with the wall clock's whole seconds and 0 nanoseconds ( kern_clock_gettime ). What the runtime does. It answers the clocks whose meaning FreeBSD fixes and the host has: - CLOCK_REALTIME (0) and CLOCK_SECOND (13), from the host's wall clock; - CLOCK_MONOTONIC (4), from the host's monotonic clock. What stops by name: other clocks and a missing timespec. Their errors go through errno , which the runtime does not model. sceKernelClockGettime(id, tp) is the same call under its SCE name. It returns 0x80020000 plus the error number: EINVAL for another clock and EFAULT for a missing timespec, as FreeBSD answers them. The executable's call ( 0x0111a815 ) asks for clock 4, and treats anything but 0 as failure.
docs.title: clock_gettime and sceKernelClockGettime (libkernel, issue #34)

docs.text: uint64_t sceKernelGetProcessTime(void) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares it, is the time since the process started. Its unit is microseconds. The executable turns it into seconds by dividing by 1,000,000: - at 0x00e4fb6e , through the compiler's multiply by 0x431bde83 and shift by 50; - at 0x0252607e , through a division by the double 1000000.0. It also seeds a random generator with it ( 0x00835dba ). What the runtime does. It measures from its own start, on the host's monotonic clock.
docs.title: Process time (sceKernelGetProcessTime, issue #34)

docs.text: The audio job manager (libSceAjm) decodes compressed audio in batches of jobs. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Ajm.h names these two calls without signatures, so their shapes come from the executable's only calls: - 0x01118a65 : runs while its context variable still holds -1, and passes 0 and the variable's address. A nonzero result is failure. - 0x01118a81 : then passes that context, 1 and 0, and again treats nonzero as failure. What the runtime does. It hands out a context id and records the registered module. Decoding belongs to the batch and instance calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: - a nonzero first argument to initialize; - a module other than the observed 1 (which codec it names is not public); - a nonzero third argument; - a context the runtime did not hand out; - registering a module twice.
docs.title: Audio job manager start-up (sceAjmInitialize, sceAjmModuleRegister, issue #37)

docs.text: The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's AudioOut.h declares int32_t sceAudioOutInit(void) and int32_t sceAudioOutOpen(user, port type, index, length, sample rate, param) . Its _types headers give: - port type 0 (main); - format 4 (float stereo); - the error codes 0x8026000E (already initialized) and 0x8026000F (not initialized). What the executable does: - Its only init call ( 0x0111b665 ) accepts success or exactly 0x8026000E . - Its only open ( 0x0111b69d ) passes user 0xff (the system user in the SDK's user types), the main port, index 0, 256 samples, 48000 Hz and a format. It keeps a non-negative result as the port handle. - The format is the executable's own evidence. Its output callback ( 0x0111b600 ) accepts 2 or 8 channels and passes 4 | (channels == 8) . So 4 is float stereo (as in the SDK) and 5 is float with eight channels. The boot opens eight channels. - A second open ( 0x0111b6fc ) passes port type 1 with the same settings, and does not check the result. The PS4 name of type 1 is not public; the sibling Vita SDK calls it BGM. What the runtime does. It records each open port and hands out handles from 1. Sound output belongs to the output calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: any open other than the observed ones, and running out of handles. int32_t sceAudioOutSetVolume(handle, flag, int32_t *volume) , as the SDK declares it, comes next. The executable's only call ( 0x0111b6d6 ) passes its new port, flag 0xff and eight volumes of 32768, and treats nonzero as failure. Flag bit n selects channel n, whose volume is volume[n] . What the runtime does. It records the volumes. What stops by name: - a handle it did not hand out; - a flag naming a channel the port does not have; - a missing array; - a volume outside 0–32768. int32_t sceAudioOutOutput(handle, const void *samples) , as the SDK declares it, hands a port sound. The executable's audio thread ( 0x0111b93c ) hands its port one block at a time ( length samples for every channel). It advances its ring buffer when the result is not negative, and loops with no wait of its own. So the call itself paces the thread: it returns once the port has room for the next block. What the runtime does. It plays nothing yet. - Each port takes one block per length / rate seconds (256 samples at 48000 Hz: 5.33 ms). - A call waits until the block before it would have finished playing, then answers 0 (the caller only checks the sign). - A port that falls behind starts again from now. What stops by name: a missing block, and a handle the runtime did not hand out.
docs.title: Audio output (sceAudioOutInit, sceAudioOutOpen, sceAudioOutSetVolume, sceAudioOutOutput, issue #37)

docs.text: scePthreadAttrSetschedparam(attr, const struct sched_param *param) sets the priority ( sched_param 's one int) of a thread created with the attribute. OpenOrbis' libkernel.h gives the shape; libthr's _pthread_attr_setschedparam gives the semantics. What the executable does. Its thread wrapper ( 0x0111aafd ) sets it without explicit-scheduling inheritance. So under libthr's default ( PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED ), the new thread still starts at its creator's priority. The wrapper then sets the priority itself with scePthreadSetprio ( 0x0111ab46 ). What the runtime does. It records the priority on the attribute. A variable holding no attribute is EINVAL (libthr). What stops by name: a missing param, and a priority outside 256–767. scePthreadAttrSetaffinity(attr, uint64_t mask) is the wrapper's next call ( 0x0111ab0e ), with the CPU mask its caller chose. As for scePthreadSetaffinity , the runtime records the mask (the created thread takes it) and the host schedules. An empty mask stops by name, and a variable holding no attribute is EINVAL .
docs.title: Attribute priority and CPU mask (scePthreadAttrSetschedparam, scePthreadAttrSetaffinity, issue #34)

docs.text: The title reads its own data under /app0 , the console's read-only mount of its package. The runtime serves /app0 from your own copy and never writes to it: - tools/boot.py --app0 DIR chooses the copy, defaulting to $BB_APP0 , then $BB_DATA_ROOT/merged . - pbboot takes it as --app0 . - A path under any other mount, and one with a .. component (which could leave the copy), stops by name. sceKernelStat(path, struct stat *) is FreeBSD's stat(2) under its SCE name, which returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. The PS4 's struct stat is FreeBSD 9's amd64 layout, 120 bytes (OpenOrbis' _types/kernel.h , OrbisKernelStat ). What the executable does. Its call at 0x02474519 asks whether /app0/dvdroot_ps4/sound/sprj_mixer.fev exists: - 0 means yes; - exactly 0x80020002 ( ENOENT ) means no; - anything else goes to its error path. What the runtime does. It fills the structure from the host file: - type, size, block count and size, link count and times; - the permission bits without write (the mount is read-only); - device and inode numbers as the host's (they only identify the file); - the birth time as the modification time (the host's stat has none); - owner, group, flags and generation 0. Errors. A missing file answers ENOENT , and a missing directory component ENOTDIR (the same numbers on FreeBSD and Linux). Any other host error stops by name.
docs.title: The title's files: /app0, sceKernelStat, opening and reading (issue #35)

docs.text: sceKernelOpen , sceKernelRead , sceKernelPread , sceKernelLseek , sceKernelFstat and sceKernelClose are FreeBSD's open(2) , read(2) , pread(2) , lseek(2) , fstat(2) and close(2) under their SCE names. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares the shapes. Each returns a result, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. The executable opens its data with flags 0 ( O_RDONLY ) and mode 0555. What the runtime does: - Opening. It opens the host file read-only. A request to write, create, truncate or append answers EROFS , as FreeBSD does on a read-only mount. The lookup comes first: a missing file without O_CREAT is ENOENT . Other flag bits stop by name. - Descriptors. A descriptor is the runtime 's own number, from 3 up, standing for a host descriptor (the title only passes it back). One the runtime did not hand out is EBADF . - Seeking. A whence other than 0, 1 or 2 ( SEEK_SET , SEEK_CUR , SEEK_END , the same on FreeBSD and Linux), and a seek before the start, are EINVAL .
docs.title: Opening and reading

docs.text: Implement the established contract and test the RT_SYSLIB entry through its library and symbol name. Keep target-specific values separate from host values. When an argument, ID, return value, or error case is unknown, fail loudly with the call name and leave the question open; never choose a value to make tools/boot.py advance.
