docs.text: 6 October 2026: from an empty repository to the frame loop The first day: the target was prepared, the repositories and tooling were set up, and the first Ghidra export and verified frame-loop replacements were completed, from the clock up to the function that runs every frame. The target Both packages extracted without keys and merged. The update's param.sfo reports the 1.09 app version. All eight executables (the eboot and seven PRX modules) were fake-signed SELFs with no encrypted segments, and converting them to ELF only unwrapped them. Hashes are on the Target page. Repositories and tooling progress.py derives every number from symbols/ in the code repository. verify.py runs the original code and a replacement side by side, outside the game, on the same inputs, and compares everything they do (more on that below). The pre-commit hooks refuse game data, local notes and stale progress numbers. The converted eboot has no section headers, so there is no .text to measure. The progress denominator is the set of functions Ghidra finds in executable blocks, tied to the hash of the committed export. The first Ghidra export Ghidra 12.0.3 with the GhidraOrbis loader imported the eboot and finished full auto-analysis in about 26 minutes. It found 157,757 functions in .text , 42,487,347 bytes, not counting 9,302 thunks . All 671 imports resolved to names through the NID database. The loader decides where .text ends with a heuristic, and on a small module it put almost all the code into .rodata , where nothing gets analyzed. So the export needed a check that does not depend on Ghidra at all: the unwind table. It lists 162,959 functions. 155,000 of them are functions in the export, and the other 7,959 are all thunks , which the export skips on purpose. Ghidra also found 2,757 functions that have no unwind entry. The gap is fully accounted for. That is the size of the job: about 158 thousand functions and 42 MB of code. The first function: a millisecond clock 0x0111a7f0 turned out to be a monotonic millisecond clock: it asks the system for CLOCK_MONOTONIC , keeps the seconds of its first call in a shared state object, and returns the milliseconds since then. The C++ replacement does the same, down to the 32-bit arithmetic that wraps. To check the checker, deliberately broken versions of each replacement are run through verify.py ; each must fail. Then the game runs with the hook installed, the replacement records its real inputs as it goes, and those recordings are compared too: over 30,000 calls in 90 seconds here, and the game reached the title menu exactly as it does without the hook . Two bugs were caught before anything was marked verified : the recording code dropped half of each clock value, and the tester counted cases from two runs as one when they shared names. With the monitors off, the desktop throttles a game window to one frame a second. A virtual display ( Xvfb ) fixes that for test runs, at about 15 frames a second on the title screen. Finding the frame limiter The plan was to walk outward from the millisecond clock to the frame limiter. But the clock and its two neighbours have 52 callers, all in one stretch of the executable and none touched by any frame-rate patch: a separate subsystem, not the frame loop. The frame-rate patches by Kyo (and Lance McDonald for the uncapped one) were written by people who already found the limiter. Mapping every patched address to its function, then keeping the functions that both read the clock and sleep, left one that every frame-rate patch edits: 0x02434770 , now frame_timing_pace_frame . The frame limiter article explains how it works. The limiter, replaced , and the first option The replacement follows the original instruction by instruction, down to how it converts between integers and floating point and how each comparison treats NaN. Twenty-six hand-written cases cover every mode; four deliberately wrong versions all fail, after two of them first got through and showed the cases had blind spots. In-game recordings, with the community patches off so the original is the real one, all match. The spinning wait broke the first recording: frames with more than 20,000 clock reads were dropped, which removed exactly the frames that spin. Runs of clock reads are now stored as one series. BB_TARGET_FPS set to 30 , 60 or uncapped changes the limiter in code, the way the community patches change it with byte edits. Unset, nothing changes. It covers only the limiter: the patches also fix many places where the game assumes 30 frames a second, and those still need the patch until they are replaced too. BB_LIMITER_WAIT=sleep makes the limiter sleep instead of spinning while it waits. Both wait for a measurement on a real screen. The frame step and the flipper frame_timing_frame_step is the function the main loop calls once per frame. It asks the window object whether the game is still running, creates the frame-pacing object on the first frame, runs the limiter, runs the game's task update, and asks two more objects whether the player has asked to quit. Four of those questions are virtual calls, so it was the first function whose inputs are objects: the recordings now describe each object as a small stand-in whose table slot points at the real function the game called. It matched on every recorded frame. frame_timing_flipper_init builds the frame-pacing object. It reads the config value Game.FlipMode twice through the game's own string class; the shipped config leaves it unset, which is why the game runs the 30 FPS mode. Verified on the recorded call and nine edge cases . The microsecond time helper the frame-rate patches edit is replaced too, but the game never calls it before the title menu, so it waits for a run that gets further. The frame-rate option, corrected A function nothing calls turned out to be a code cave: the time helper the frame-rate patches edit is never called in the stock game, and the patches overwrite it with their own code. That led to a closer look at what the patches do to the functions we did replace, by disassembling each with and without the patch. They do more than the limiter: they also make the frame step hand the game the measured frame time instead of a fixed 1/30 s. Our hooked frame step had switched that off, so the first version of BB_TARGET_FPS=60 would have run the game logic twice as fast. The test harness can now apply a patch to the original code, so each part of the option is checked against the patch itself: all edge cases , every deliberately wrong version caught, and frames recorded at 60 FPS in the game match. A real-screen measurement waits for the display plug. Counting calls, and three more functions Of the 59 functions the frame-rate patches touch outside frame timing, 12 turned out to be dead code and 47 live. To find which of the live ones the game actually runs, the runtime can now count calls to original functions without replacing them: a short jump at each entry to a counter that then runs the original. One gameplay run in Iosefka's Clinic showed 13 of them running, several every frame. Nine of the others are small state methods that advance an owner by a fixed 1/30 s step; they are built next to the game's Chalice Dungeon singleton and do not run in the clinic. They are replaced and checked against the 60 FPS patch, and wait for a save that reaches the Chalice Dungeons. A per-frame task that hands the frame time to its parts is replaced and verified , including what the uncapped patch does to it through a code cave. And the engine's condition variable wait is the first function of a new system, the engine's kernel layer: the patches put a return over its timed wait that would crash if it ran, and every wait the game made was untimed. One trap on the way: Ghidra treats the engine's fatal error as a call that never returns, so it hides the instructions right after it. The game's code does continue there, and a replacement written from the listing alone got one path wrong until the bytes were read directly. Workflow The work no longer waits on the maintainer between steps: a target queue, a standing procedure, a smoke test of the whole pipeline at the start of each session, a lock that keeps two projects off the GPU at the same time, and one game run records inputs for every replaced function at once. Checking the limiter's recordings used to keep a core busy for four minutes; with a native answer for the clock reads, the executable loaded once and low priority, it takes under one. Replacements may start from a draft of the decompiler's output, kept on the maintainer's machine and never committed. What is committed is the renamed, readable, verified version. This wiki The site theme and the one-post-per-day devlog were established alongside the project's documentation. Next The live functions the 60 FPS patches edit, starting with the frame-time descriptor family. The other places the frame-rate patches edit.

docs.text: 7 October 2026: a new direction, our own runtime Paleblood opened its code to contributors and began building a clean-room runtime of its own. This entry combines the day's runtime work and decompilation progress. Runtime and boot progress Earlier that day, the former runtime ran the game at 60 FPS through Iosefka's Clinic. The project then began removing that borrowed runtime and its graphics dependency. Paleblood's new loader maps the executable byte for byte and its verification harness reproduced the earlier function results. At this point the new runtime did not run the game; its system-library work stopped at an unimplemented import. The roadmap still included threads and memory, files, input, audio, video out, and graphics. Decompilation and verified functions The frame-loop work included the pad manager's step, reference-counted render updates, present/ vblank handling, YEBIS sample parameters, six task-manager functions, a physics constructor, the Havok AI manager, and a character update. Existing cases cover per-frame work and 19 physics constructions. The AI manager's branches and idle paths use explicit test fixtures. Tests caught floating-point edge cases , stack arguments, thread-local state, shared patch data, and object memory that the harness needed to describe. Tooling and automation The verification harness learned to pass and return floating-point values, model stack arguments and thread-local state, apply the frame-rate patch to the original, and count calls without replacing functions. Deliberately incorrect replacements were used to check that the cases caught known mistakes. The project also introduced a readable-code review gate and a contributor route based on claimed work and pull-request evidence. Documentation and website changes The public Paleblood repository opened with contribution guidance and protected pull requests. The runtime roadmap and clean-room boundary were documented alongside the new loader . Tests and validation The verification harness ran existing recorded and edge cases , and deliberately wrong versions exposed several test gaps. The new loader reproduced the same verification results. These checks validated function behavior; they did not demonstrate full game execution on the project-owned runtime . Blockers and next steps At the time, the new runtime still needed its system imports and execution layers before it could boot the game. The decompilation continued independently, with every replacement requiring recorded inputs where available, edge cases , readable code, and matching verification evidence.

docs.text: 9 October 2026: a path for runtime contributors Runtime-only contributors can implement a documented syscall without access to a game dump or recorded captures . This day's work prepared the issue #34 contribution route and clarified what the current boot evidence does and does not establish. Runtime and boot progress The runtime still stopped at its first unresolved system call. The maintainer's boot check runs locally after a runtime pull request merges; a contributor does not need proprietary files or captures to implement and test a runtime -only change. Decompilation and verified functions No function replacement or verification status changed in this milestone. The frame limiter's clock calls pass a null timezone to gettimeofday ; a separate sceKernelClockGettime call uses clock ID 4 , but the IDs passed to the imported clock_gettime are still unknown. Those gaps remain open instead of being filled with assumed return values. Tooling and automation The issue #34 workflow uses a claim-and-branch process, small related changes, and a concise evidence report. Paleblood PR #44 , merged at ef1989e , prepared the contributor checks. Runtime-only pull requests use the compiler matrix, system-library tests, and policy checks. Decompilation and mixed changes retain the full session report and verification gates. Shared Git hooks dispatch through the active worktree, so linked worktrees use their own installed checks. The devlog moved to one post per day: new milestones are added to that day's post under fixed sections, and repeat updates replace their own entry instead of adding a second one. The publishing script keeps the Paleblood source it builds from separate from the public site. This is workflow only; the game did not get further. Paleblood PR #51 makes the boot history record where each run stopped (the phase, the unresolved import and where the game faulted), even when only that location changes between runs. This improves diagnostics; it is not boot progress. Documentation and website changes The syscall notes distinguish public contracts for getpagesize , getpid , clock_gettime , and gettimeofday from target-specific behavior not yet established. The loading map records the bundled Fios module while leaving archive access, PlayGo flow, and target-specific error paths as open questions. Progress was synchronized from merged Paleblood sources. Paleblood PR #52 notes that running the full game still depends on the old borrowed runtime until Paleblood has its own equivalent checks. Byrgenwerth removed the pages, test-run media and build hook left over from that runtime , and added checks so they don't come back. Tests and validation The issue #34 workflow added no replacement and no verification result. Runtime-only CI checks run without game data; pull-request CI validates the changed code and policy before the local post-merge boot check. The shared hook changes were exercised in linked worktrees. Blockers and next steps The first unresolved import and the target-specific behavior listed above still need evidence. The next runtime change should implement one documented call or a tightly related group, keep unknown behavior explicit, and include deterministic tests and its source basis. Nine functions are checked against hand-written edge cases , but none of them has matching recordings from the game yet, so none could be promoted to verified . Issue #34 is still claimed by a contributor and is still the earliest boot blocker. Issues #35–#40 are open, but they don't yet describe the system calls well enough to implement them safely. docs.text: 10 October 2026: recorded verification and runtime foundations This day improved capture reliability, verified one function from existing recorded calls, and added four deterministic network byte-order imports. The tooling work did not itself advance game execution. Runtime and boot progress Paleblood PR #50 , merged at 816ea96 , added sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs . These implement fixed-width host/network byte-order conversions; socket, resolver, epoll, and online behavior remain uncovered. The saved boot result still stopped at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (238/686 system imports provided), within contributor-owned issue #34. No boot run was made for this change. Paleblood PR #55 adds Paleblood's own version of the callback that redirects a game function to its replacement. A synthetic test confirms the redirect works. The full game run still uses the old runtime , which doesn't call this yet. Decompilation and verified functions Paleblood PR #48 promoted frame_timing_pace_frame ( 0x02434770 ) using its existing evidence: 585/585 recorded calls and 26/26 edge cases . Its approved independent review remained in place. PR #49 refreshed generated public documentation from the merged verification result; it added no runtime behavior or new cases. The verified function count reached 21. Tooling and automation Paleblood PR #46 made capture output stable, recorded function/run provenance, refused unsafe paths and existing case files, and kept older schema-1 cases replayable. PR #47 added an isolated typed adapter proof with explicit signature and memory descriptors. Synthetic fixtures passed capture , serialization, replay, and verification; unsupported signatures and missing descriptors failed closed. Production replacements still do not call this adapter, so these tests produced no real game captures . Paleblood PR #53 lets the runtime issue counts see implemented system calls without waiting for a boot run. That corrected issue #41 : its network group now shows the four byte-order helpers from PR #50, 4/175 implemented. Paleblood PR #54 adds a test that checks how Paleblood talks to the old runtime : version checks, handing over the game image, registering redirects and passing errors back. It guards against regressions; nothing new runs. PR #55 also made the repository's Git hook tests more robust: they respect the configured temporary directory and stop cleanly if their test copy can't be made. The tests confirm that the hooks refuse game code and block a push when a required check fails. Documentation and website changes The frame-timing page and generated progress data were refreshed from merged Paleblood revision 816ea96 . The public site was published at 21e1d26 . The runtime notes keep the production observer and capture integration explicitly unfinished. Public source documents the synthetic limits alongside the results. All 30 public wiki pages were reviewed against the current Paleblood source, and the Runtime, Architecture and CI Setup pages were updated; the Runtime page now lists the four network byte-order helpers. Automatic syncing from Paleblood stays off until it can run with safe, limited credentials. The first Workshop article explains the verified per-frame character points update ( 0x01cbdb20 ): how it keeps fractional amounts between frames, its limits, and the evidence behind it, with a diagram. Calling it "stamina" is still a guess, and the article says so. A redesign put the wiki's pages into seven themed, collapsible menu groups that remember which ones you opened and work as a drawer on phones. The homepage got the hunter artwork chosen by the maintainer (SteamGridDB, by r_dsgnd ) in place of a product image. The redesign went live at public site commit 975ec0c . Every page loaded, the search index was up to date, and the phone menu opened, closed and moved focus correctly. The sidebar menu was repaired and the artwork moved into it, above Home, with its credit beneath. Section headings line up and no longer wrap, submenus sit along a guide line, only one section opens at a time, and short windows scroll instead of squeezing the menu. The homepage now opens with Master Willem's words. The repaired menu went live at public site commit 6b16b45 , with the artwork in the sidebar and no longer on the homepage. Tests and validation The capture changes passed GCC and Clang builds and all 11 CTest suites. The verification promotion used the 585 recorded calls plus 26 edge cases . The four network helpers passed registry tests with known byte patterns, zero, maximum-width values, and round trips; both compiler builds and all 11 CTest suites passed. Clean-room, policy, hook , and session audits also passed. Blockers and next steps No production capture integration or game execution advanced. 0x02713870 still has no matching recorded inputs and remains blocked. The earliest saved boot blocker remains the issue #34 affinity import; synthetic capture tests are not substitutes for matching recorded cases or production ABI evidence. docs.text: 11 October 2026: more imports supplied, same boot blocker Two genuine boot traces raised the supplied system imports from 238 to 247 of 686, but startup still stops at the same call, scePthreadAttrGetaffinity . The day also re-checked the millisecond clock against the original code, documented IPv4 text conversion, and published the roomier sidebar menu. Runtime and boot progress A traced boot run ( tools/boot.py --trace ) on the local Bloodborne executable, using Paleblood PR #61 on top of merged main 251d426 , resolved 246/686 imports: 219 from bundled game modules and 27 implemented by Paleblood. It reached seven import calls and stayed at loaded (0/8), stopping at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , the same blocker as the earlier 238/686 baseline. The eight extra imports come from merged PRs #50 and #59 and a corrected count of unresolved imports; startup did not advance. A second boot run on merged Paleblood main 68d5f93 resolved 247/686 imports (219 bundled, 28 runtime ): PR #63 supplies one more. It still reached seven import calls and stopped at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (0/8). This was the real game executable in the boot harness , not a gameplay run. Decompilation and verified functions The catalog is unchanged at 21 verified , 30 replaced , and 30 edge-verified functions. No function was promoted today. Tooling and automation The differential harness ran the original instructions of the millisecond clock ( 0x0111a7f0 ) beside Paleblood's replacement: all 1,767 recorded inputs and 10 edge cases matched. This repeats the evidence for an already- verified function, so the counts did not change. No executable or capture data was added to the repository. Documentation and website changes The roomier sidebar menu is live at public site commit e691994 . Submenus sit along a guide line with more space between entries, and one section opens at a time. The sidebar now shows the menu artwork alone; its credit and copyright notice moved to the Credits page. With PR #61 merged, the Runtime pages now note that sceNetCtlGetInfo and sceNetCtlGetNatInfo are callable but deliberately fail loudly, so they no longer count as implemented. This corrects the coverage numbers; it is not startup progress. The Runtime pages also explain the new sceNetInetPton support (IPv4 text conversion only), what evidence backs it, and the limits of its synthetic tests. The network group in issue #41 now stands at 9/175 implemented imports. Tests and validation Fresh GCC and Clang builds passed, with 13/13 CTest cases each. The session audit, hook tests, game-data policy, progress consistency, and function validation checks all passed. Blockers and next steps scePthreadAttrGetaffinity is still the first unresolved call and the earliest boot blocker; it is tracked in contributor-owned issue #34. Once it lands, the next boot run will show how far startup gets past the loaded stage. docs.text: Week of 19 October 2026: A bounded verification pipeline and a clearer site The documentation caught up with merged tracing, control-flow feedback and the opt-in automation prototype, the runtime numbers followed the newest merged boot record, and the site got a new menu. None of it establishes a new verified function or startup milestone. Runtime and boot progress Catching up on 11–15 October. @clee 's merged PR #66 makes getpagesize stop by name under both import names instead of guessing. The game's own executables bound the answer to a divisor of 16384 (4096, 8192 or 16384), and no public source says which one the PS4 reports, so only a console observation can settle it. The entries do not count as implemented. @EzequielRindello 's merged PR #62 compares guest thread handles, and PR #72 supplies the documented sched_yield path. scePthreadYield stays unresolved because its PS4 return signature is unknown. The registry tests are synthetic. No boot was run for this audit; the saved result still stops at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , before the first startup milestone. merged #82 runtime : implement memcpy and memset (libSceLibcInternal) , by @EzequielRindello . Merged 2026-10-19. System calls: memcpy; memset. Tests: 2 synthetic runtime test(s); the effect on the real boot is measured after merge, so this is not a boot result. Left unresolved: PS4 C library behavior for undefined cases (overlapping memcpy regions, null pointers) is not modelled. merged #81 runtime : implement scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate , by @BluePinetree . Merged 2026-10-19. System calls: scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate (libkernel); pthread_attr_setdetachstate (libScePosix); rt_thread_attr_detach_state (internal reader for thread creation). Tests: 4 synthetic runtime test(s); the effect on the real boot is measured after merge, so this is not a boot result. Left unresolved: the PS4 detach state of a fresh attribute: the reader stops by name; the PS4 detach state of an attribute filled by scePthreadAttrGet: the reader stops by name; null or empty variable meaning the defaults at thread creation is libthr behaviour; the runtime stops in both cases; the reader has no production caller until scePthreadCreate is implemented; pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy (POSIX names) are not registered yet. Merged PR #82 , by EzequielRindello, adds registry-backed memcpy and memset . Merged PR #81 , by BluePinetree, adds detach-state setters and a reader that fails loudly for an unknown system default. Focused synthetic registry tests support these changes; neither merge is a new game boot or verified -function promotion. Source reviewed: 2e5da0854d999c486f4310ba0b7b055d4e939f36 . merged #83 runtime : report stub modules loaded at run time , by @adurham . Merged 2026-10-20. No function status changed. Decompilation and verified functions Catching up on 11–15 October, which fell between the daily posts and the first weekly one. @ThisIsAkill 's merged PR #64 replaces event_flag_write : a lookup by flag group picks direct or strided storage, then sets or clears the flag's bit. All 14 authored edge cases match the original, so it is edge-verified , not verified : no game recording reaches it yet, and finding the save state that does is the open question. No function was implemented, promoted, or newly verified during this documentation audit. The generated baseline remains 21 fully verified and 31 cumulative replaced / edge-verified functions. The AI article now limits its claim to the verified shared-world wrapper; it does not claim that individual enemy or boss decisions have been decoded. Existing original-instruction evidence was not rerun. Tooling and automation Catching up on 11–15 October. @ThisIsAkill 's merged PR #65 adds a function catalog that ranks research candidates from static call and instruction data, and PR #67 qualifies those candidates by ownership and evidence, so a candidate without ownership evidence stays conditional rather than queued. Merged Paleblood PR #70 supplies fixture replay, bounded exploration, mismatch minimization, and evidence bundles. PR #74 adds supported guest-instruction memory observations; #75 corrects POP's stack-relative destination, and #76 rejects classified unsupported instruction families. #78 adds bounded block/edge feedback, and #79 coordinates a qualified candidate, prewritten replacement, local fixtures, checks, and an opt-in draft PR. Synthetic success establishes tool behavior. Skipped host code still makes a trace incomplete; no complete real-game candidate-to-PR run is established. merged #80 diagnostics: identify incomplete harness import traces , by @ThisIsAkill . Merged 2026-10-19. Findings: The recorded frame timing canary exits guest tracing at the sceKernelClockGettime harness bridge; the host dispatcher remains unobserved and the trace is incomplete.. Merged PR #80 names incomplete harness import traces and preserves the original execution result. This improves diagnostics, not game execution. docs.text: The Great Ones The research map for boss encounters. Paleblood has not yet identified any boss's internal decision tree or phase code. Profiles Boss Directory What evidence an individual boss profile needs. Read Behavior Boss AI & Phases Visible encounter changes versus the unverified state machines that may cause them. Read Combat Boss Mechanics Attacks, damage, stagger, and arena interactions without turning an impression into a code claim. Read What a boss encounter is made of A boss fight brings together many systems that are studied separately elsewhere: an entity's updates, animation, attack effects, collision, damage, arena events, and the player's response. Start with the evidence we have AI. Paleblood has verified a wrapper that steps the shared Havok AI world. Its internal world update and individual enemy decisions remain unknown. The AI system page explains exactly what that wrapper proves. Other shared systems. The Character , Event , and Physics pages describe other verified pieces that could eventually intersect a boss encounter. They do not yet identify boss-specific behavior. What this page can and cannot claim Every claim in this section is labelled by the kind of evidence behind it. Label Meaning observed Seen during play or in a recording, with its context: starting state, player position and actions, the visible change, and whether it repeats. inferred A conclusion drawn from code or tests, stated with the scope that evidence covers. unknown Not yet traced. It stays an open question, with the evidence needed next. Observation is not implementation. An animation, health-bar change, phase transition, hit reaction, movement, or line of dialogue can be observed. On its own it does not identify an entity ID, function, data field, condition, timer, probability, script, or internal state. No guessing. Nothing is filled in from genre convention, a gameplay impression, animation timing, or a displayed bar. Visually similar actions are not assumed to share code. No guessed names, IDs, catalogs, or numerical tables are published. What a source claim needs. The entity, the function and address, the data or state it reads, the result it produces, public Paleblood source at the exact merged revision, tests, and independent review. Evidence kinds differ. Recorded original-game behavior, static analysis, synthetic Paleblood tests, and verified replacements are different kinds of evidence. A link to one does not prove the others. Tests have a scope. Passing tests support equivalence on the cases they cover, not untested gameplay situations. Timing and probability claims need measurements or directly verified logic, not a single encounter. Shared systems are not specific actors. The verified AI, Character, Event, and Physics findings do not yet identify any particular boss, enemy, NPC, weapon, or attack. Absence is not a claim about the game. A missing profile describes the project's research, not what the game contains. See Evidence & Media Review for how this wiki labels evidence.

docs.text: AI. Paleblood has verified a wrapper that steps the shared Havok AI world. Its internal world update and individual enemy decisions remain unknown. The AI system page explains exactly what that wrapper proves. Other shared systems. The Character , Event , and Physics pages describe other verified pieces that could eventually intersect a boss encounter. They do not yet identify boss-specific behavior. What this page can and cannot claim Every claim in this section is labelled by the kind of evidence behind it. Label Meaning observed Seen during play or in a recording, with its context: starting state, player position and actions, the visible change, and whether it repeats. inferred A conclusion drawn from code or tests, stated with the scope that evidence covers. unknown Not yet traced. It stays an open question, with the evidence needed next. Observation is not implementation. An animation, health-bar change, phase transition, hit reaction, movement, or line of dialogue can be observed. On its own it does not identify an entity ID, function, data field, condition, timer, probability, script, or internal state. No guessing. Nothing is filled in from genre convention, a gameplay impression, animation timing, or a displayed bar. Visually similar actions are not assumed to share code. No guessed names, IDs, catalogs, or numerical tables are published. What a source claim needs. The entity, the function and address, the data or state it reads, the result it produces, public Paleblood source at the exact merged revision, tests, and independent review. Evidence kinds differ. Recorded original-game behavior, static analysis, synthetic Paleblood tests, and verified replacements are different kinds of evidence. A link to one does not prove the others. Tests have a scope. Passing tests support equivalence on the cases they cover, not untested gameplay situations. Timing and probability claims need measurements or directly verified logic, not a single encounter. Shared systems are not specific actors. The verified AI, Character, Event, and Physics findings do not yet identify any particular boss, enemy, NPC, weapon, or attack. docs.text: Boss AI & Phases A boss can visibly change its movement, attacks, or presentation mid-fight. This page explains what is known about the code behind that, and how a visible change becomes a code-level explanation. At a glance What is verified ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 advances the shared Havok AI world by a fixed 1/30-second step. What is open The AI world update at 0x021cdad0 , its groups and objects, and individual enemy behavior. Boss-specific No state machine, phase trigger, attack choice, or cooldown has been reverse engineered. What the verified wrapper does Each frame, ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 : advances the shared Havok AI world by a fixed 1/30-second step; conditionally copies matrices; conditionally draws debug information. Its tests and recordings establish the wrapper's behavior, not the AI world's internal decisions. The update inside it, at 0x021cdad0 , is where boss decisions would live, and it is still unmapped ( AI system findings ). Observation is not implementation A visible change cannot, by itself, tell us whether a threshold, event, timer, distance check, or random choice caused it. A phase boundary seen in a video, for example, does not establish the field or branch that controls it. To record an encounter for a future study, write down: Record Example of what to note Starting state Where the fight was when the sequence began Player position and actions What the player was doing Visible transition What changed on screen Repeatability Whether it happens again under the same conditions Keep that as an observation. Do not turn it into a claim about a hidden threshold or probability without source evidence. What decompilation must establish To explain a boss phase in implementation terms: Find the entity and the update path that runs it. Trace the transition condition and the data it reads. Verify any claimed timing or attack selection. Cite the exact merged source revision and relevant tests or review records. If only the transition is observable, label it as observed and leave its cause unknown. The Boss Directory has the full profile requirements. docs.text: AI The game runs a shared Havok AI world, owned by the SprjHkAiManager singleton. This page covers the once-a-frame update that steps that world and draws its debug display. At a glance Scope The per-frame AI manager update: the world step and the AI debug drawing. Verified ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 steps the AI world by a fixed 1/30 s and gates the debug drawing behind flags. Open The world step itself ( 0x021cdad0 ), the groups and objects, and how individual enemies decide what to do. Summary The game steps a shared Havok AI world through SprjHkAiManager (singleton 0x059401a0 ). The verified wrapper does not establish which enemy or NPC decisions that world supplies. What one frame does Once a frame, ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 ( 0x0222bc10 ): Steps the Havok AI world with a fixed time step of 1/30 s. Checks its second flag. It is always set in the recordings. When it is set, the update: copies the frame object's matrices to the manager's view object; resets the render manager's debug state to its defaults and runs the AI debug display and drawing, made of the pieces below. Piece What it uses Debug position the camera's position, or the player character's when the character manager exists Debug marks (not yet detailed) Draw descriptor every AI object in the owner's groups, or the whole manager Axis frames ids looked up in the manager's id map Boxes the box mode at +0x2c68 The time step is a constant, not the measured frame time. Every frame moves the AI world on by 1/30 s however long the frame really took. That is why the frame-rate patches have to change it (see Patch points ). In the recordings from Iosefka's Clinic the update resets its three groups, copies the matrices and draws each AI object; the debug display, axis frames, boxes and the manager-wide draw stay off. Scope still to map: the AI world step itself ( 0x021cdad0 ), the groups and objects, the behaviour of individual enemies. What this wrapper does not tell us This verified wrapper establishes how the AI manager is stepped and how its debug drawing is gated. It does not reveal an individual enemy's decisions, attack timing, or boss phases. The current source and evidence contain no basis for those profiles yet; gameplay observations alone will be labeled as observations until their implementation is traced. docs.text: Once a frame, ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 ( 0x0222bc10 ): Steps the Havok AI world with a fixed time step of 1/30 s. Checks its second flag. It is always set in the recordings. When it is set, the update: copies the frame object's matrices to the manager's view object; resets the render manager's debug state to its defaults and runs the AI debug display and drawing, made of the pieces below. Piece What it uses Debug position the camera's position, or the player character's when the character manager exists Debug marks (not yet detailed) Draw descriptor every AI object in the owner's groups, or the whole manager Axis frames ids looked up in the manager's id map Boxes the box mode at +0x2c68 The time step is a constant, not the measured frame time. Every frame moves the AI world on by 1/30 s however long the frame really took. That is why the frame-rate patches have to change it (see Patch points ). In the recordings from Iosefka's Clinic the update resets its three groups, copies the matrices and draws each AI object; the debug display, axis frames, boxes and the manager-wide draw stay off. Scope still to map: the AI world step itself ( 0x021cdad0 ), the groups and objects, the behaviour of individual enemies. What this wrapper does not tell us This verified wrapper establishes how the AI manager is stepped and how its debug drawing is gated. It does not reveal an individual enemy's decisions, attack timing, or boss phases. The current source and evidence contain no basis for those profiles yet; gameplay observations alone will be labeled as observations until their implementation is traced.

docs.text: Character Every character instance in the game is updated once a frame. This page covers one of those updates: throw events, the regeneration of a points stat, and the hand-off of frame time to the character's modules. At a glance Scope character_frame_update_01cbdb20 , one of the per-frame updates of a character instance. Verified character_frame_update_01cbdb20 is verified : the throw event, the points regeneration with its fractional carry, and the frame-time hand-off. Open Whether the points stat is stamina, whether the update belongs only to the player, and the rest of the instance layout. Summary Character instances ( ChrIns in FromSoftware's engine) are updated once a frame through virtual calls on each instance. character_frame_update_01cbdb20 ( 0x01cbdb20 ) is one of these updates. What the update does Fires a pending throw animation event ( W_ThrowAtk or W_ThrowDef ) and clears the request. Regenerates a points stat that floors at -50 and caps at a maximum (see below). It reads like stamina. Hands the frame time to the character's modules , copies a few parameters, and builds (then drops) a wide string of the character's name with the thread's allocator. Nothing reads the string; it looks like the remains of debug code. In the recordings from Iosefka's Clinic the name string is never built. How the points stat regenerates The regeneration rate is a product of four terms: Text Only rate = parameter byte × 0.01 × per-character multiplier × virtual factor The multiplier lives at +0x16c on the instance, and the last rate is kept at +0x39c . Each frame the update: multiplies the rate by the frame time (read from +0xe0 ); adds the whole part of the result to the points (data module +0x134 ), capped at the maximum ( +0x138 ); keeps the fraction at +0x168 and adds it in on the next frame. Carrying the fraction means a rate too small to add a whole point in one frame still adds up over several frames instead of being rounded away. Two switches stop the stat from dropping: bit 7 of the data module's +0x200 , and the debug flag 0x0593e88a next to the WorldChrManDbg singleton. Points, stamina and the player The source calls this value points . Its relationship to stamina, and whether this update belongs only to the player, are not established. The current evidence-backed account is in Stats & Progression . Scope still to map: the character instance layout, the modules ( +0x3b0 ), the parameters, the other per-frame updates. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x01cbdb20 979 character_frame_update_01cbdb20 verified per-frame character update: throw animation event, points stat regeneration (stamina-like, -50..max), time-step descriptor; the 30/60 FPS patches fix its frame time Structs and globals Character instance Offset Field +0x58 -> +0x38 parameters +0xe0 frame time +0x168 regeneration fraction +0x16c multiplier +0x350 name +0x39c last rate +0x3b0 modules Data module ( modules +0x20 ): points +0x134 , maximum +0x138 , a no-drop flag at bit 7 of +0x200 . 0x0593e88a : a debug flag (next to the WorldChrManDbg singleton 0x0593e880 ) that stops the stat from dropping. Patch points The frame-rate patches (see Frame timing ) replace the frame time read from +0xe0 with a constant: Patch Frame time used 30 FPS++ 1/27 s 60 FPS++ 1/54 s 60FPS (no deltatime) 1/50 s 90 FPS++ 1/80 s Uncap FPS++ the real frame time BB_TARGET_FPS does the same for 30 and 60. A fixed time slightly longer than one frame (1/27 instead of 1/30) speeds regeneration up a little; why the patch authors chose it is an open question. Open questions Is the points stat stamina? A floor below zero would fit a stat that can be overspent. Why the patches choose 1/27 and 1/54 rather than 1/30 and 1/60.

docs.text: Event The event system keeps the game's event entries, runs its Lua event scripts and stores its event flags. This page covers how an event entry is found or added, and how one event flag bit is written. At a glance Scope SprjEmkSystem (event entries), SprjLuaEventMan (Lua event scripts) and SprjEventFlagMan (event flags). Verified event_emk_add is verified ; event_flag_write is edge-verified against constructed cases. Open What the two entry lists hold, what the ids mean, and what any real flag ID means in play. Summary The game's event system is three managers working together: Manager What it keeps SprjEmkSystem event entries, kept in keyed lists SprjLuaEventMan the Lua event scripts SprjEventFlagMan event flags Adding an event entry event_emk_add ( 0x016efd00 ) is the way into the entry lists: It looks for an event entry by id and sub-id in two linked lists. If there is none, it allocates, constructs and inserts one in key order. It advances a new entry once by a fixed 1/30 s step. It runs hundreds of times in a minute of gameplay in Iosefka's Clinic. Writing an event flag event_flag_write ( 0x017cfcc0 ) changes one stored bit. Flags are stored in groups, so the function first works out which group holds the flag, then which bit in that group: It divides the flag ID by the store's configured flags-per-group value. It finds an exact matching group in a keyed tree. It selects either a direct storage pointer or a stride-based offset into shared storage. It sets or clears the bit. Within a byte, flags are numbered from the most significant bit; a nonzero enabled argument sets the selected bit and zero clears it while retaining its neighbors. A missing group, unsupported storage kind, or null storage pointer leaves memory unchanged. This replacement is edge-verified , not fully verified : it matches the original on constructed edge cases , not on recorded gameplay. How the flag write was verified The merged source and layout and verification record report matching original-instruction results on 14 constructed edge fixtures. Those cover tree search paths, byte boundaries, set/clear operations, missing groups, and storage selection. What the fixtures do not establish They do not identify a real flag ID's gameplay meaning, establish a zero group-size contract, or replace recorded gameplay cases. No fixture was rerun for this article. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x016efd00 368 event_emk_add verified SprjEmkSystem: find or add an event entry in two keyed lists; first advance with the 1/30 s step (1/60 s in the 60 FPS patches) 0x017cfcc0 177 event_flag_write edge-verified finds an exact event-flag group in a tree and sets or clears one bit Structs and globals Event entry (0xe0 bytes): Offset Field +0x0 vtable; slot +0x10 advances the entry by a frame-time descriptor +0x28 id +0x2c sub-id (16-bit) +0x70 next entry Patch points 60 FPS++ , 60FPS (no deltatime) and 90 FPS++ change the first advance's 1/30 s step to 1/60 s in 0x016efd00 ; BB_TARGET_FPS=60 does the same. The patches are described in Frame timing . Open questions What the two lists hold (pending and active entries?), and what the ids are.

docs.text: Frame timing How the game paces its frames: a frame step that runs once a frame, a frame limiter that waits out each frame's budget, and a task manager that runs the frame's work. At a glance Scope Frame pacing, delta time, vsync and the main loop's time step. Verified The frame step, the frame limiter, the flipper constructor and the task manager's frame path are replaced and verified . Our option BB_TARGET_FPS does in code what the community frame-rate patches do in these functions. Open A few limiter fields, the owner of the 0x0111a... clock layer, and most functions the 60 FPS patches edit. Summary next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work The frame step frame_timing_frame_step ( 0x02418d20 ) runs once per frame. In order, it: checks that the SprjWindow is running; creates the SprjFlipper singleton on first use ( frame_timing_flipper_init , 0x02434520 ); runs the frame limiter, frame_timing_pace_frame ( 0x02434770 ), a method of that flipper; runs the task update with a small 1/30 s descriptor; asks a quit gate and a quit query, and returns whether the game keeps running. Both the limiter and the frame step are replaced and verified . The frame limiter Each frame the limiter does four things. It applies the flip mode. The constructor reads the mode from the config value Game.FlipMode . A pending mode at +0xc replaces the current one at +0x8 when +0x276 is set. The mode chooses the sync interval (stored at +0x10 ) and the frame interval (a float at +0x18 ): Flip mode Sync interval Frame interval 0 and 1 2 1/30 s 2 1 1/60 s 3 and 4 1 1/30 s It reads the time with gettimeofday , in microseconds. It waits out the frame's budget , shortened when recent frames ran late. A switch in the build ( 0x013e3980 , always 1) selects the spinning wait, which polls the clock without sleeping (hundreds of thousands of reads in a long frame). A sleeping wait is compiled in but unused. It keeps the last 32 frame times in a ring (index at +0x260 ) and derives a frame rate from their average ( +0x2b8 ). Which clock the game reads gettimeofday supplies wall time, so it is not guaranteed to be monotonic. The frame limiter's confirmed call passes a null timezone pointer. The game's separate verified clock helper invokes sceKernelClockGettime with ID 4 , identified as CLOCK_MONOTONIC ; that does not establish the IDs accepted by the imported libc clock_gettime wrapper. See the runtime system-call notes . Two other clock functions are easy to mistake for part of the limiter: 0x004632d0 is a small gettimeofday helper in microseconds that the stock game never calls: nothing calls it directly, and no relocated pointer (vtable or table slot) points at it. The frame-rate patches overwrite it and its neighbours with their own code (a code cave), so it is not replaced . The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 are not on the limiter's path. They look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem. Correction (2026-10-06): the 0x0111a... clocks are a separate layer The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 are not on the limiter's path. All 52 of their callers sit in one region ( 0x0110e... - 0x0121b... ) that shares its own helpers, and no frame-rate patch touches any of them: they look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem (unidentified; possibly middleware). Their system label may move once that subsystem is known. Frame time in game logic The frame step also passes time into character updates. One verified update accumulates a per-frame points value using that time and retains fractional progress between frames. Its evidence and unresolved stat identity are documented in Stats & Progression . The task manager's frame Each frame, the frame step hands the frame's work to FD4::FD4TaskManager (singleton 0x058b2e30 ). The path is a good example of how an engine brackets its work so that nothing runs twice or half-finished: 0x024512a0 fetches the task manager and runs every task group ( 0x01388c60 , mask -1 ). 0x01388c70 refuses to start while a frame is already running (a busy flag at +0x38 ). It flushes the task queue that collected work since the last frame ( 0x0143e490 : lock, run each queued object, destroy and free it, empty the list, unlock), steps the worker threads' queues ( 0x014400a0 ), and publishes the frame's value ( 0x0143f9f0 copies a float from the frame's information to a global). With the busy flag set, it calls the dispatcher ( +0x40 , virtual +0x30 ), which runs the frame's tasks; then it clears the flag, flushes the second queue and steps the workers again. The dispatcher ( 0x0138a370 ) is the last link: when its group record asks for it, it wakes every registered task (76 in Iosefka's Clinic), then fills a job with the record, the task table and the group mask and runs it through the same five steps as the workers. Each of those tasks is a piece of the game's own per-frame work, the next layer to map. Every override is skipped: the reset flag ( +0x2c4 ), the two override counters ( +0x2bc , +0x2c0 ) and the two clear flags ( +0x271 , +0x272 ). At the end the sync interval ( +0x10 ) is kept on late frames instead of zeroed. Frame step ( 0x02418d20 ): the frame time passed to the task update starts at 1/60 s (30: 1/30 s), and when the flipper's interval is not 1/30 s it becomes the measured frame time ( +0x264 ) clamped to [interval, 1/30 s]. This is the patches' delta time: the game logic advances by how long the frame really took. The patch drops the SprjTask check to make room. Flipper constructor ( 0x02434520 ): the first interval is 1/60 s (60 and 90). They also edit 59 other functions; 12 of them are dead code in the stock game (no caller, no relocated pointer). Many of the rest pass the same 1/30 s frame-time descriptor to an owner object, which the 60 FPS patches change to 1/60 s. The patches also rewrite dozens of shared constants in the data segment (the 1/30 s step at 0x04d29170 becomes 1/60 s, 1/90 s or, uncapped, 1/60 s), which code we have not replaced reads too. BB_TARGET_FPS covers only the replaced functions, so it is meant to run together with the patch; option checks run both sides on the patched image for that reason. How the patch edits were mapped tools/patch_overlap.py maps every patch line to the function it falls in, and lists the patches that do nothing while our hooks are installed. Our option: BB_TARGET_FPS BB_TARGET_FPS=30 , 60 or uncapped does in code what 30 FPS++ , 60 FPS++ and Uncap FPS++ do in the three functions above. Unset keeps the original behaviour exactly. The option has to cover the frame step as well as the limiter. A faster limiter alone would still tell the game logic that every frame lasts 1/30 s; the delta time comes from the frame step (see the patch points above). The other functions the patches edit are not replaced yet, so a 60 FPS game would still need the community patch for them; its edits inside our three functions do not run, and our option does their part. A second option, BB_LIMITER_WAIT=sleep , makes the limiter use the sleeping wait the game carries but never selects: it sleeps until about 5 ms before the frame's end and spins the rest, so a fast machine does not keep a core busy waiting. How the option is checked against the patches Each part is checked against the patch itself: tools/verify.py run --patch FILE:NAME --env BB_TARGET_FPS=... runs the original with the patch's bytes applied against our replacement with the option, on the edge cases and on frames recorded in the game at 60 FPS. Recorded frame times at 60 FPS (October 7) A saved October 7 measurement with the external host scaffold, all replacements hooked, and BB_TARGET_FPS=60 reports a median frame time of 16.67 ms and p99 of 16.69 ms. That historical result is recorded in Paleblood's status evidence ; it is not a real-display result from Paleblood's project-owned boot path. History: the first version changed only the limiter An earlier version only changed the limiter. Because the hooked frame step no longer ran the patches' delta-time code, at 60 FPS the game logic would still have been told every frame lasts 1/30 s; checking against the patches found that, and that the limiter's own settings differed. Open questions What +0x14 and the counters at +0x268 / +0x26c mean (the latter set how many recent late frames the catch-up sums). Which subsystem the 0x0111a... clock layer belongs to. What each live function the 60 FPS patches edit belongs to, and which run in gameplay.
docs.title: Frame timing

docs.text: How the game paces its frames: a frame step that runs once a frame, a frame limiter that waits out each frame's budget, and a task manager that runs the frame's work. At a glance Scope Frame pacing, delta time, vsync and the main loop's time step. Verified The frame step, the frame limiter, the flipper constructor and the task manager's frame path are replaced and verified . Our option BB_TARGET_FPS does in code what the community frame-rate patches do in these functions. Open A few limiter fields, the owner of the 0x0111a... clock layer, and most functions the 60 FPS patches edit.
docs.title: Frame timing

docs.title: Summary

docs.text: frame_timing_frame_step ( 0x02418d20 ) runs once per frame. In order, it: checks that the SprjWindow is running; creates the SprjFlipper singleton on first use ( frame_timing_flipper_init , 0x02434520 ); runs the frame limiter, frame_timing_pace_frame ( 0x02434770 ), a method of that flipper; runs the task update with a small 1/30 s descriptor; asks a quit gate and a quit query, and returns whether the game keeps running. Both the limiter and the frame step are replaced and verified .
docs.title: The frame step

docs.text: Each frame the limiter does four things. It applies the flip mode. The constructor reads the mode from the config value Game.FlipMode . A pending mode at +0xc replaces the current one at +0x8 when +0x276 is set. The mode chooses the sync interval (stored at +0x10 ) and the frame interval (a float at +0x18 ): Flip mode Sync interval Frame interval 0 and 1 2 1/30 s 2 1 1/60 s 3 and 4 1 1/30 s It reads the time with gettimeofday , in microseconds. It waits out the frame's budget , shortened when recent frames ran late. A switch in the build ( 0x013e3980 , always 1) selects the spinning wait, which polls the clock without sleeping (hundreds of thousands of reads in a long frame). A sleeping wait is compiled in but unused. It keeps the last 32 frame times in a ring (index at +0x260 ) and derives a frame rate from their average ( +0x2b8 ).
docs.title: The frame limiter

docs.text: gettimeofday supplies wall time, so it is not guaranteed to be monotonic. The frame limiter's confirmed call passes a null timezone pointer. The game's separate verified clock helper invokes sceKernelClockGettime with ID 4 , identified as CLOCK_MONOTONIC ; that does not establish the IDs accepted by the imported libc clock_gettime wrapper. See the runtime system-call notes . Two other clock functions are easy to mistake for part of the limiter: 0x004632d0 is a small gettimeofday helper in microseconds that the stock game never calls: nothing calls it directly, and no relocated pointer (vtable or table slot) points at it. The frame-rate patches overwrite it and its neighbours with their own code (a code cave), so it is not replaced . The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 are not on the limiter's path. They look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem. Correction (2026-10-06): the 0x0111a... clocks are a separate layer The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 are not on the limiter's path. All 52 of their callers sit in one region ( 0x0110e... - 0x0121b... ) that shares its own helpers, and no frame-rate patch touches any of them: they look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem (unidentified; possibly middleware). Their system label may move once that subsystem is known.
docs.title: Which clock the game reads

docs.text: The frame step also passes time into character updates. One verified update accumulates a per-frame points value using that time and retains fractional progress between frames. Its evidence and unresolved stat identity are documented in Stats & Progression .
docs.title: Frame time in game logic

docs.text: Each frame, the frame step hands the frame's work to FD4::FD4TaskManager (singleton 0x058b2e30 ). The path is a good example of how an engine brackets its work so that nothing runs twice or half-finished: 0x024512a0 fetches the task manager and runs every task group ( 0x01388c60 , mask -1 ). 0x01388c70 refuses to start while a frame is already running (a busy flag at +0x38 ). It flushes the task queue that collected work since the last frame ( 0x0143e490 : lock, run each queued object, destroy and free it, empty the list, unlock), steps the worker threads' queues ( 0x014400a0 ), and publishes the frame's value ( 0x0143f9f0 copies a float from the frame's information to a global). With the busy flag set, it calls the dispatcher ( +0x40 , virtual +0x30 ), which runs the frame's tasks; then it clears the flag, flushes the second queue and steps the workers again. The dispatcher ( 0x0138a370 ) is the last link: when its group record asks for it, it wakes every registered task (76 in Iosefka's Clinic), then fills a job with the record, the task table and the group mask and runs it through the same five steps as the workers. Each of those tasks is a piece of the game's own per-frame work, the next layer to map.
docs.title: The task manager's frame

docs.text: Input The input system handles the controller pads. This page covers the once-a-frame step of FD4PadManager, the manager that keeps a map of pad entries. docs.text: Kernel The engine's core library: thin wrappers around the PS4 kernel for threads, mutexes and condition variables, which report every unexpected result through one fatal error function. At a glance Scope Dantelion2's kernel layer ("ClassLibrary/Core/Kernel" in its source paths), and the kernel and libc calls the executable imports. Verified kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ), the condition-variable wait the frame-rate patches edit. Open Which objects the condition waits made each frame belong to. Summary What the kernel layer is Dantelion2 is the engine's core library. Its kernel classes wrap the PS4 kernel's threads, mutexes and condition variables. Each wrapper checks the result of the call it makes, and any unexpected result goes to the engine's fatal error function ( 0x024b55b0 ), which takes a file, a line and a message. How a condition wait works kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ) waits on a condition variable. It has two paths: Timeout of -1 : it waits forever (an untimed wait). Any other timeout : it makes a timed wait, and returns -3 if the time runs out. It is called about 40 times a frame in gameplay. Every wait recorded in gameplay is untimed, which matters for the frame-rate patches (see Patch points ). Imports are not implementations The executable and its bundled libc import POSIX-like calls such as getpagesize , getpid , clock_gettime and gettimeofday . An import only says the game can call something; it does not mean Paleblood implements it. For implementation status and evidence limits, see the runtime system-call notes . Two clock details are established so far: The frame limiter passes null as gettimeofday 's timezone argument. Numeric clock ID 4 is confirmed for sceKernelClockGettime , not for the imported clock_gettime wrapper. getpagesize: why it stops by name In the current runtime , both getpagesize entries are registered as fail-loud unresolved diagnostics because the PS4 page-size value is not established, as recorded in merged Paleblood PR #66 . Runtime thread-call implementations These are Paleblood runtime services, not newly decompiled game functions: the runtime answers some thread and timing calls itself. Two rules run through them: A call is implemented only when its guest-visible contract is known. Where the PS4 's exact behaviour is not established, the call stays a fail-loud diagnostic that stops by name. The SCE names and the POSIX names of the same call differ in their errors: the POSIX names return the FreeBSD error number, where the SCE names return 0x80020000 plus it. The current boot stop, scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , remains unimplemented until the main thread's real affinity mask is established. None of these changes has been verified by a new Bloodborne boot. What each runtime change implements (PRs #62, #72, #81, #94, #95, #97) Merged PR #62 implements scePthreadEqual by comparing the object pointers used as guest thread handles. Its synthetic registry tests cover one handle compared with itself, distinct handles in both argument orders, and null; the public FreeBSD pthread_equal(3) contract supports zero for unequal and nonzero for equal, but the PS4 's exact nonzero value is unknown. Merged PR #72 implements imported sched_yield by yielding the host thread and returning zero, following POSIX and FreeBSD's documented contract. Unit tests check the result but cannot show that another host thread actually ran. Later runtime merges extend the same thread and timing group: PR #81 adds the detach-state setters for thread attributes under both the SCE and POSIX names. Reading a detach state that the system itself supplies still stops by name, because the PS4 default is not established. PR #95 registers the POSIX names pthread_self , pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy . They return the FreeBSD error number where the SCE names return 0x80020000 plus it. PR #94 sleeps the host thread for sceKernelUsleep , the call the verified frame limiter and swap-chain present functions make, and for usleep below one second. PR #97 ends the program by name on __stack_chk_fail . These are runtime services checked by synthetic registry tests, not decompiled game functions. scePthreadYield is not implemented The similarly named scePthreadYield remains registered as an unresolved, fail-loud diagnostic. FreeBSD's pthread_yield returns void , Linux's analogue returns int , and no PS4 declaration or inspected guest call site settles the guest-visible signature. Do not infer that it is implemented from its registry entry. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x02483e80 204 kernel_condition_wait verified Dantelion2 PthreadCondition wait (untimed when timeout is -1); the FPS patches put a ret on the timed path Structs and globals Not documented yet. Patch points 30 FPS++ , 60 FPS++ , 90 FPS++ and Uncap FPS++ write a return over the timed-wait call in 0x02483e80 . If that path ever ran, the return would jump to a garbage address. Every wait recorded in gameplay is untimed, so it never does. Our replacement keeps the original behaviour. Open questions Which objects the ~40 condition waits per frame belong to (job queues, the render thread?).

docs.text: Physics The game's rigid bodies live in one physics world: shared tables of bodies, motions and constraints that other objects index into, and listeners that hear when a body changes. At a glance Scope The physics world reached through the physics manager, and the objects that own bodies in it. Verified The physics-instance constructor physics_instance_construct_01c0c2b0 ( 0x01c0c2b0 ). Fixed step An instance's controller steps at 1/30 s; the 60 FPS patches and BB_TARGET_FPS=60 make it 1/60 s. Open What kind of object a physics instance is, and what the manager's two special modes mean. Summary The physics world The game keeps its rigid bodies in a physics world reached through the physics manager ( 0x0593d700 → +0x28 → +0x8 ). The world holds tables that everything else indexes into: Table Offset in the world Entry size (bytes) Bodies +0x20 0x90 Motions +0xe0 0x80 Constraints +0x128 0x38 Listeners (told when a body changes) +0x538 list How a physics instance is built physics_instance_construct_01c0c2b0 ( 0x01c0c2b0 ) is the constructor of a physics instance : an object that owns a set of bodies in that world (a ragdoll or a breakable object would look like this; which one is still open). Reading it is a good lesson in how a constructor wires a new object into shared tables: It asks the body-set constructor for its bodies, then moves every active body (flags +0x40 & 3 ) by the offset it was given. It writes a 16-byte back-link for each of its bodies and constraints, and points the world's tables at them, so the world can find the instance from any body. It copies the set's shape table ( 0x30 bytes per shape) into a buffer from a dedicated heap, handing it to a shape object, and builds a controller whose fixed frame step is 1/30 s and whose transform starts at the root body. Unless the physics manager is in one of its two special modes (as it is while Iosefka's Clinic loads), it rescales each active body's four 16-bit motion values and tells the world's listeners about each body, removing listeners that are flagged for removal. Last, it creates its own listener and a tracker, and collects the distinct motion types above 4 of its bodies. How the motion values are rescaled The four values are stored as the top halves of 32-bit floats (the format known as bfloat16): 16 bits holding a float's sign, exponent and the top of its mantissa. Step 4 above works like this: Widen. Each value goes back to a float by putting it in the upper half of a float's bit pattern. Scale. The first three are multiplied by 0.2, and all four by 1.00390625. Narrow. Only the top 16 bits of each result are kept again (an arithmetic shift of the bit pattern, then a saturating pack). It is a compact way to store floats at half the size, and an example of why a replacement has to reproduce the exact instructions: the truncation works on the float's bits, not its value. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x01c0c2b0 3222 physics_instance_construct_01c0c2b0 verified physics instance constructor over a body set: back-links, shape copy, controller (step 1/30 s; 60 FPS patches 1/60), motion rescale, listeners Structs and globals Object Field Meaning Physics manager ( 0x0593d700 ) +0x28 → +0x8 The world +0x274 , +0x275 Special-mode flags World +0x20 Body table +0xe0 Motion table +0x128 Constraint table +0x538 Listener list (a tagged pointer: the low two bits are flags) Body ( 0x90 bytes) +0x30 Position +0x40 Flags +0x68 Motion index +0x88 Back-link Instance +0x38 Body set +0x70 / +0x78 Back-links +0x88 Shape object +0x90 Controller (frame step at +0x60 ) +0x128 Own listener Patch points The controller's frame step is 1/30 s; 60 FPS++ (and 90 FPS++ , 60FPS (no deltatime) ) make it 1/60 s. BB_TARGET_FPS=60 does the same. Open questions What kind of object is a physics instance: ragdolls, breakables, or both? What do the physics manager's two special modes mean? docs.text: The game keeps its rigid bodies in a physics world reached through the physics manager ( 0x0593d700 → +0x28 → +0x8 ). The world holds tables that everything else indexes into: Table Offset in the world Entry size (bytes) Bodies +0x20 0x90 Motions +0xe0 0x80 Constraints +0x128 0x38 Listeners (told when a body changes) +0x538 list
docs.title: The physics world

docs.text: physics_instance_construct_01c0c2b0 ( 0x01c0c2b0 ) is the constructor of a physics instance : an object that owns a set of bodies in that world (a ragdoll or a breakable object would look like this; which one is still open). Reading it is a good lesson in how a constructor wires a new object into shared tables: It asks the body-set constructor for its bodies, then moves every active body (flags +0x40 & 3 ) by the offset it was given. It writes a 16-byte back-link for each of its bodies and constraints, and points the world's tables at them, so the world can find the instance from any body. It copies the set's shape table ( 0x30 bytes per shape) into a buffer from a dedicated heap, handing it to a shape object, and builds a controller whose fixed frame step is 1/30 s and whose transform starts at the root body. Unless the physics manager is in one of its two special modes (as it is while Iosefka's Clinic loads), it rescales each active body's four 16-bit motion values and tells the world's listeners about each body, removing listeners that are flagged for removal. Last, it creates its own listener and a tracker, and collects the distinct motion types above 4 of its bodies.
docs.title: How a physics instance is built

docs.text: The four values are stored as the top halves of 32-bit floats (the format known as bfloat16): 16 bits holding a float's sign, exponent and the top of its mantissa. Step 4 above works like this: Widen. Each value goes back to a float by putting it in the upper half of a float's bit pattern. Scale. The first three are multiplied by 0.2, and all four by 1.00390625. Narrow. Only the top 16 bits of each result are kept again (an arithmetic shift of the bit pattern, then a saturating pack). It is a compact way to store floats at half the size, and an example of why a replacement has to reproduce the exact instructions: the truncation works on the float's bits, not its value.

docs.text: Render The render system draws each frame and presents it to the screen. This page covers three mapped pieces: the per-frame render update, the pacing of each present, and one helper from the YEBIS post-processing middleware. At a glance Scope render_frame_update_02377bd0 , render_swap_chain_present and render_yebis_get_recursive_sample_parameters . Verified All three: the reference-counted object list, the vblank pacing of the present, and the blur sample counts. Open What the listed objects and the two children are; draw submission, GNM command buffers, shaders, post-processing. Summary The per-frame update render_frame_update_02377bd0 ( 0x02377bd0 ) runs once a frame: It walks a list of reference-counted objects and updates each one. An object whose update says it is finished loses its reference (destroyed at the last one; an underflow is reported as "DLReferenceCountObject: Invalid Unref() call"), and its node is unlinked and freed. It updates a RendMan -side child ( RendMan : singleton 0x05940298 ). It steps another child by a frame time of 1/30 s, or 0 while that child is held. Pacing the present render_swap_chain_present ( 0x025b2fb0 , the graphics framework's GXSwapChainCtrl ) paces each present: It waits until the requested number of 60 Hz vblanks has passed since the last present. It sleeps until 17 ms before that time, then polls the clock. It maps the interval to a flip mode. It presents. In Iosefka's Clinic the game presents with interval 1 and does not wait here; the frame limiter sets the pace. Blur sampling (YEBIS) render_yebis_get_recursive_sample_parameters ( 0x00fbc3e0 ) belongs to YEBIS, the post-processing middleware. Its GPUTexUtil_GetRecursiveSampleParameters works out: how many recursive passes a blur needs; how many samples the last one takes; how far apart the first one samples. It carries the middleware's own assertions. Scope still to map: draw submission, GNM command buffers, shaders, post-processing. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x00fbc3e0 670 render_yebis_get_recursive_sample_parameters verified YEBIS GPUTexUtil_GetRecursiveSampleParameters: blur pass count, last-pass samples and scale; the FPS patches drop its first assertion 0x02377bd0 399 render_frame_update_02377bd0 verified per-frame: ages a list of ref-counted objects, updates RendMan-side child, steps another child by 1/30 s (Uncap: measured frame time) 0x025b2fb0 768 render_swap_chain_present verified GXSwapChainCtrl present: waits for the present interval in 60 Hz vblanks, maps it to a flip mode, presents (Uncap: mode 0) Structs and globals The update's owner Offset Field +0x10 list sentinel (next +0x0 , prev +0x8 , object +0x10 ) +0x18 count +0x20 allocator (frees nodes through vtable slot +0x70 ) +0x70 child, stepped through vtable slot +0x40 +0x80 child +0x8c the held flag +0x98 a byte copied into the +0x70 child each frame Reference-counted objects : vtable slot 0 destroys, count at +0x8 (atomic). Patch points The frame-rate patches are described in Frame timing . Uncap FPS++ makes the +0x70 child's step the flipper's measured frame time ( +0x264 ) whatever the held flag says, through a small code cave inside the function, and drops the RendMan check. The 1/30 s it reads otherwise is the shared constant at 0x04d29170 , which the 60, 90 and uncapped patches rewrite in the data segment. Uncap FPS++ presents with flip mode 0 (no vblank sync) at the end of 0x025b2fb0 . Every frame-rate patch removes the first assertion of 0x00fbc3e0 (at least 3 base samples): at higher frame rates the blur gets fewer samples. Open questions What the reference-counted objects in the per-frame list are, and what the two children are. Draw submission, GNM command buffers, shaders and post-processing have not been studied yet.

docs.text: Movement & Stamina Movement and resource use are easy to observe during play. Their internal representation and update rules need source evidence, so this page keeps the two levels separate. At a glance What is verified character_frame_update_01cbdb20 ( 0x01cbdb20 ) updates a bounded field the source calls points . Not established That points is player stamina, that the function is player-only, or how movement consumes the value. Unknown Locomotion, dodge distance, acceleration, lock-on movement, and stamina use and recovery as one mechanic. How the verified points update works Each frame, character_frame_update_01cbdb20 : multiplies a rate by the frame time; adds the whole portion of the result to points ; retains the fraction for a later frame; applies a lower bound and a per-instance maximum. The tests cover recorded and generated inputs across the documented timing variants. The evidence does not establish that points is player stamina, that the function is player-only, or how movement consumes the value. See the full evidence account and the Character system . What remains unknown No verified current function explains player locomotion, dodge distance, acceleration, lock-on movement, or stamina consumption and recovery as a connected mechanic. docs.text: Stats & Progression One verified per-frame character update changes a bounded value the source calls points . It is a concrete example of how a game stat can be driven by the frame loop. At a glance Function character_frame_update_01cbdb20 ( 0x01cbdb20 ), called from two character update loops. What it does Accumulates fractional recovery between frames, applies a character-specific rate, and clamps the result between -50 and a per-character maximum. Status Verified against recorded original-game calls and generated edge cases , with independent review. Not established That points is the player's stamina, that it belongs only to the player, or how it fits the wider progression system. This article describes one function and its tested behavior. It is not a complete account of combat, weapon costs, attributes, leveling, or save data. The per-frame update character_frame_update_01cbdb20 ( 0x01cbdb20 , 979 bytes) is called from two character update loops. In order, it: reads the character's frame time; handles a pending throw animation event when the animation-event manager is ready; updates the points value (below); passes time into a character module step; runs other module calls and copies data used by the character and animation systems. The Character page lists the observed fields and remaining layout questions. How points change each frame Check the flag. If the character parameter flag disables regeneration, return without changing the stat. Work out the rate. Multiply the parameter byte by 0.01 , the character multiplier, and a factor returned through the character's virtual table. The result is the per-second rate. Add this frame's share. Save the rate truncated toward zero, then calculate frame time × rate + saved fraction . Split whole and fraction. Apply the whole-number portion to the current points value and keep the fractional remainder for the next update. Guard and clamp. If the change would lower points, skip it when the data flag or observed debug flag disables drops. Otherwise clamp the value to at least -50 and at most the character's maximum. Why keep the fraction? It stops each frame from discarding the part of the recovery smaller than one point. A slower update can therefore accumulate several fractional contributions before the integer stat changes. The points field's game-facing identity is unresolved. Frame-time variants The update normally uses the frame time stored on the character. The community frame-rate patches substitute their own: Mode Frame time the update uses Original timing The frame time stored on the character Community 30 FPS patch 1/27 second Community 60 FPS patch 1/54 second Uncapped patch The stored time Paleblood's BB_TARGET_FPS option mirrors those substitutions in this function. See Frame timing for the main loop and the broader patch comparison. Those constants explain the code path; they do not establish why the patch authors selected them or how the resulting rate feels in every game state. How we know The replacement is marked verified in Paleblood's function table. It was compared against two kinds of evidence, in each of four runs (original timing, 30 FPS, 60 FPS, uncapped): Recorded cases: previously captured original-game calls. Edge cases: generated boundary cases. Each comparison reported zero failures, and an independent review approved the readable refactor after rerunning all recorded and edge cases . These results support equivalence over those recorded inputs and generated cases. They do not prove every possible state, identify the points value as stamina, or establish that an enemy or boss uses this exact update. See Evidence & Media Review for how this wiki labels different kinds of evidence. Verification record and source links The verification record, dated 2026-10-07 with source digest b243fddb1ca6589a , reports 457/457 recorded cases and 39/39 edge cases for each of four runs: original timing, 30 FPS, 60 FPS, and uncapped. Each comparison reported zero failures. An independent review record says the readable refactor was approved and all recorded and edge cases were rerun. docs.text: Weapons & Transformations A transformed weapon is a visible change in how an equipped weapon looks and is used. That change is a starting point for research, not proof of the internal state layout, attack table, or transition function. At a glance What is verified Nothing about weapon instances, transformation states, weapon-specific attack selection, or the functions that switch forms. Easy to misread The character update can fire W_ThrowAtk or W_ThrowDef throw-animation events. That is not transformation evidence. Not published No weapon catalog or numerical attack table without verified evidence. The throw-animation event The verified character update can fire a pending throw-animation event named W_ThrowAtk or W_ThrowDef . That is the only weapon-adjacent behavior in the current evidence, and it says nothing about weapon transformation logic. Its implementation and limits are described in Character and Stats & Progression . What a source-backed profile needs Connect a weapon identifier to its state data and update path. Establish the transition conditions. Trace the animation/event handoff and attack selection. Measure any timing or resource effects. Record observable transitions separately from source-derived explanations. If the code does not yet show whether a property is shared across weapons, leave that question open.
